0.title: A Farewell Letter from the Rock
0.overview:
Second Peter is the apostle's last will and testament. Writing in the shadow of his own death — 'the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me' (1:14; cf. John 21:18–19) — Peter addresses a church under pressure from false teachers who have crept inside the community, twisted Paul's letters, and weaponized a crude uniformitarianism against the hope of Christ's return. The letter's three movements answer three threats: the erosion of moral seriousness (ch. 1: grow in the divine nature), the corruption of doctrine by immoral teachers (ch. 2: their condemnation is certain), and the mocking of eschatological hope (ch. 3: the Day is coming and it will be unlike anything the world has seen).

The letter's authorship is the most contested in the NT canon. The vocabulary differs sharply from 1 Peter, and Origen already noted that some doubted it. Eusebius placed it among the antilegomena — letters known but disputed. Yet the arguments for Petrine authorship are substantial: the self-identification is unusually specific (Simeon Peter, v.1; the eyewitness claim of vv.16–18; the reference to a prior letter in 3:1); a forger who fabricates this much personal detail is extraordinarily bold. The vocabulary difference most likely reflects a different secretary — 1 Peter was written dia Silouanou (through Silvanus, 1 Pet 5:12), while 2 Peter's quite different style may reflect Peter writing without that help, or with another. The church ultimately recognized it as canonical, and its theological weight — the virtue chain, the transfiguration testimony, the patience of God, the new creation — fully justifies that recognition.

The relationship to Jude is unavoidable: 2 Peter 2 and Jude share extensive material (the angels who sinned, Sodom and Gomorrah, the Balaam archetype, waterless clouds, the scoffers of the last days). The majority of scholars believe Peter used Jude (not the reverse), which, if correct, places 2 Peter after Jude and in the mid-to-late 60s AD — consistent with Peter's death under Nero (c. 64–68 AD). Peter does not merely copy Jude; he develops, expands, and re-focuses the material for a church whose crisis has moved from external pressure to internal corruption.

1.title: Partakers of the Divine Nature
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ:<sup>2</sup>May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.<sup>3</sup>His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence,<sup>4</sup>by which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire.<sup>5</sup>For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge,<sup>6</sup>and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness,<sup>7</sup>and godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love.<sup>8</sup>For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>9</sup>For whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins.<sup>10</sup>Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall.<sup>11</sup>For in this way there will be richly provided for you an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.<sup>12</sup>Therefore I intend always to remind you of these qualities, though you know them and are established in the truth that you have.<sup>13</sup>I think it right, as long as I am in this body, to stir you up by way of reminder,<sup>14</sup>since I know that the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me.<sup>15</sup>And I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things.<sup>16</sup>For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty.<sup>17</sup>For when he received honor and glory from God the Father, and the voice was borne to him by the Majestic Glory, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased,"<sup>18</sup>we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain.<sup>19</sup>And we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts,<sup>20</sup>knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation.<sup>21</sup>For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
1.overview:
Chapter 1 lays the foundation. God’s power has already given believers everything they need for life and godliness (v. 3). On that gift rests the command: make every effort to add to your faith, and so confirm your calling (vv. 5, 10). Gift first, then effort: that is the grammar of grace.

The second half grounds Peter’s message in two witnesses that agree: the apostles saw Christ’s glory at the transfiguration, and the prophetic Scriptures, spoken by men carried along by the Holy Spirit, point to the same Christ and his coming day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Divine Power and Precious Promises
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter writes to believers whose faith is of equal value to his own. God’s power has given them everything for life and godliness, and his promises make them sharers in his holy nature. So they must make every effort to grow in a chain of qualities from faith to love. Those who grow are kept from fruitlessness and confirm that God has called them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Partakers of the Divine Nature

God's power has already granted everything needed for life and godliness. Sharing the divine nature means sharing his holiness, not becoming God — and growth in the qualities of verses 5–7 is how a believer confirms his calling.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter told readers who had seen nothing that their faith was of equal standing with his.

Now: When growth stalls, look first for a memory of forgiveness that has grown dim (v. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ: May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ: May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.

Meaning first. 2 Peter 1 lays the foundation for resisting false teachers: true knowledge of Christ, a growing Christian character, and the sure word of Scripture. Peter greets those who share the same precious faith through the righteousness of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ (vv. 1–2). God’s divine power has given us everything we need for life and godliness, through knowing him; through his great promises we share in the divine nature and escape the world’s corruption (vv. 3–4). So believers must make every effort to add to their faith a chain of virtues: goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, brotherly affection and love (vv. 5–7). These keep them fruitful; those who lack them are blind and have forgotten their cleansing (vv. 8–9). So be diligent to confirm your calling and election; then you will never fall, and you will receive a rich welcome into Christ’s eternal kingdom (vv. 10–11). Knowing he will die soon, as Jesus foretold, Peter wants to remind them of these things so they will remember after his death (vv. 12–15). The message is not a myth: Peter and others were eyewitnesses of Christ’s majesty at the Transfiguration and heard the Father’s voice (vv. 16–18). And the prophetic word of Scripture is a sure lamp in a dark place until the day dawns, because no prophecy came from human will; men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (vv. 19–21). It is the last word of an old fisherman who had seen the glory, and everything in it points away from himself to Christ.

The setting. Peter’s farewell letter, written as he expected to die soon (1:14), probably from Rome around AD 64–68, shortly before his martyrdom under Nero. It addresses the same churches as 1 Peter (3:1). Its main concern is false teachers within the churches who denied Christ’s return and lived immorally (chapters 2–3). Chapter 2 closely parallels the letter of Jude. The first letter was written to Christians suffering from outside; this one to Christians endangered from inside. Persecution can kill the body, but false teaching can empty a church while leaving its building full, and Peter, with the executioner not far off, judged it the greater danger.

Simeon Peter. The first word is unexpected. Not Simon, the ordinary Greek form, but Symeōn, the old Hebrew form, the name of a patriarch. It appears this way of Peter only once elsewhere in the New Testament, on the lips of James at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:14). Then both names together: the one he was born with and the one Jesus gave him, Petros, rock. A man writing his last letter signs it with his whole history: the fisherman from Bethsaida who sank in the lake, swore he did not know the man, and was restored on a beach; and the rock, which he never became by his own strength but was made by the One who named him. Every Christian carries two names like this. What we were, and what Christ has called us.

A servant and apostle of Jesus Christ. Servant first, doulos, a slave, and apostle second. Humility and authority, in that order. It is the same instinct as 1 Peter 5:1, where he called himself a fellow elder before he called himself anything else. The man who once argued about who was the greatest now introduces himself as the property of another. And the two words do not compete. Precisely because he is Christ’s slave, he can speak with Christ’s authority: an apostle is a man sent with a message that is not his, and the only way to carry such a message faithfully is to have no ambitions of your own for it.

To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours. The phrase is the whole letter’s opening kindness, and it repays care. “Obtained” (lachousin) is a word for receiving by lot: what falls to you rather than what you achieve. It was used of the lots that fell on Zechariah to burn incense (Luke 1:9), and of the share of ministry that fell to Judas (Acts 1:17). Faith is described as an allotment, a gift handed down, not a prize won (Ephesians 2:8). And “of equal standing” (isotimon) means of the same value, the same honour. This is remarkable coming from an eyewitness. Peter had seen the Transfiguration and will describe it in fifteen verses; he tells readers who have seen nothing, mostly Gentiles who never heard Jesus’ voice, that their faith is of exactly equal worth to his. There is no first-class and second-class Christianity, no lesser grade for those who came later.

My faith feels nothing like an apostle’s. How can it be equal? Because faith is not valued by its strength but by its object. A weak hand and a strong hand receive the same gift; a trembling faith in a mighty Christ saves as surely as a bold one. What is equal is not your feelings, your knowledge or your record, but the Christ you hold and the righteousness given to you. Thomas, who doubted, and the thief, who believed in his last hours, received the same Saviour as Peter. So do not measure your standing by comparing your faith with other people’s. Measure it by whom you are trusting, and grow from there.

By the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ. In Greek a single article governs both nouns, the construction that identifies them as one person. Peter calls Jesus God directly, as Paul does in Titus 2:13. Compare 1:11; 2:20; 3:18, where the same construction (“our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ”) plainly refers to one person: nobody has ever suggested that the Lord and the Saviour in those verses are two different people. It is one of the New Testament’s clearest statements of Christ’s deity, and it stands at the front door of a letter written against men who denied the Master who bought them (2:1). “Righteousness” (dikaiosynē) here carries two shades together: God’s fairness in giving the same faith to all, Jew and Gentile, apostle and newcomer, without favouritism; and the righteousness of Christ himself, by which believers are justified. The faith is equal because the righteousness is his, and it is not divided into larger and smaller portions.

May grace and peace be multiplied to you. Not merely given but multiplied, as in 1 Peter 1:2. Peter does not pray that they will have some grace, as though a measured ration were enough for the Christian life. He prays for increase, because the God who gives grace does not run short of it. Grace is God’s free favour; peace is what it produces: reconciliation with God and rest within.

In the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord. Here comes the letter’s key word. “Knowledge” (epignōsis) is full, personal, experiential knowledge, the knowing that belongs to a relationship rather than a library. It appears four times in this short letter (1:2, 3, 8; 2:20), and it is Peter’s answer to the false teachers, who were offering knowledge of another kind: secret, superior, liberating from ordinary morality. Peter does not answer them by despising knowledge. He answers by naming the true knowledge, the knowledge of God in Christ, and he says it is precisely here, in knowing him, that grace and peace grow.

Is this knowledge just a matter of learning doctrine? No, though it is never less than that. You cannot know a person while being wrong about who he is, so true doctrine matters. But Peter means knowing God the way a child knows his father: trusting him, hearing him, walking with him, and growing in that acquaintance over years. It comes through his word, through prayer, through the worship and fellowship of his people, and through obeying him and finding him faithful. A man can know a great deal about God and not know him; a simple believer may know little theology and know him truly. The aim is both: a mind that is accurate and a heart that is personally acquainted.

Textual note. 2 Peter was the most disputed book in the early church, and many modern scholars doubt that Peter wrote it, pointing to its different style from 1 Peter and its similarity to Jude. But the letter explicitly claims to be from Peter, refers to the Transfiguration as an eyewitness (vv. 16–18), mentions Jesus’ prediction of Peter’s death (v. 14), and refers to a previous letter (3:1). Differences of style may be due to different secretaries (Silvanus helped with 1 Peter, 5:12) and different subjects. The early church, after careful consideration, received it into the canon. We receive it as Peter’s, and as Scripture.

What it does not mean. “Equal standing” does not mean all believers have the same apostolic authority. It means the same saving faith, equally precious to God. Peter still writes as an apostle, and the readers still need to listen to him (3:2). Equality of faith is not equality of office.

In a sentence. From Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who through the righteousness of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ have received a faith as precious as ours: grace and peace be yours in abundance through the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.

On a Tuesday. If you have ever felt that real Christians are somewhere else, in another century, another country, or another church, and that you are an onlooker at the edge, this verse is addressed to you. Pray today as one with full standing. And if you know someone who feels like a second-class believer, the new convert with a chaotic past, the believer who cannot pray aloud, tell them what Peter told his readers: your faith is as precious as his.

For worship. Here is a Saviour who is God, and a God who is Saviour, and both are one Lord Jesus Christ. The fisherman who denied him calls himself his slave and calls him God in the same breath, and is glad to do both. And the faith that united Peter to him on the holy mountain is the same faith, given by the same hand, that unites the newest believer to him today. There is one Christ, one righteousness, one faith of equal honour, and grace that is not rationed but multiplied, because it flows from the one who never runs out.
verseByVerse.note: Peter’s farewell letter, written as he expected to die soon (1:14), probably from Rome in the mid 60s AD. “Simeon” is the Hebrew form of his name.

verseByVerse.quote: His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence, by which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence, by which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire.

His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness. Note the tense. “Granted” (dedōrēmenēs) is perfect: has given, and it remains ours. Not will supply as needed, in instalments, but already given in full. “Divine power” is the power of God at work through Christ, the same power that raised him from the dead. “All things” (panta): everything we need. “Life and godliness”: spiritual life, and the godly living that flows from it. And this sentence closes a door before the false teachers can open it. If everything necessary has been provided, then no supplementary knowledge is on offer, and anyone promising a further instalment is selling something that does not exist. We lack nothing necessary for living a godly life (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

If I have everything, why do I feel I am lacking so much? Because having and using are different things. A man may inherit a great house and live in one room of it, cold and hungry, because he has never opened the other doors. Peter does not say you already feel complete or behave perfectly; he says the resources are yours. What you lack is not a new gift but growth in using the one you have: knowing Christ better, trusting his promises more, and practising what he has already made possible. That is why the next verses call for effort. So when someone offers you a secret, a second blessing, a technique or a special experience that will finally make the Christian life work, you may answer kindly: I have been given all things in Christ, and I need to know him better, not something besides him.

Through the knowledge of him who called us. The channel is knowing a person, not acquiring information. “Knowledge” is epignōsis again, as in verse 2. And “called” (kalesantos) is God’s effectual call: not an invitation merely issued and left to us, but the summons that creates what it commands, as Jesus’ voice brought Lazarus out of the tomb. Everything comes through knowing Christ personally, not through secret teachings.

To his own glory and excellence. “Glory” (doxa) is the weight and radiance of who he is. “Excellence” (aretē) is moral excellence, goodness; the word was used of a god’s mighty deeds, and Peter used it in his first letter of the excellencies of the one who called us out of darkness into his marvellous light (1 Peter 2:9). The Greek can mean that God called us by his glory and excellence, drawn by his beauty as Peter himself was drawn when he fell at Jesus’ knees in the boat, or that he called us to share them. Probably both. And notice: it is his own glory, not a glory he distributes like a prize, but the one he possesses. He calls us into the very thing he is.

By which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises. Peter piles up superlatives. “Precious” (timia) is his own recurring word: he used it of the trial of faith, of the blood of Christ, and of Christ the living stone (1 Peter 1:7, 19; 2:4–7). “Very great” (megista) is literally greatest. What promises? Forgiveness, the gift of the Spirit, eternal life, Christ’s return, the new heavens and new earth in which righteousness dwells (3:4, 9, 13). And they are given, not dangled. God has bound himself by his word, and every one of his promises finds its Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20).

So that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature. An astonishing phrase. “Partakers” (koinōnoi) means sharers, partners, the word for business partners in Luke 5:10, where James and John were Simon’s partners in the fishing. “Divine nature” (theias physeōs). Through God’s promises believers share in God’s own moral character and life: his holiness, love and goodness. This is the new birth (1 Peter 1:23; John 3:5–6), union with Christ (John 15:4–5), being renewed in his image (Colossians 3:10; Romans 8:29). It needs stating carefully, because it has been misread in both directions. It does not mean human beings become God, or are absorbed into deity: Peter has distinguished us from him in every line, and the Creator-creature distinction is never negotiable anywhere in Scripture. Nor is it a poetic exaggeration meaning nothing much. God’s own life is truly in his people.

How can a promise make me share God’s nature? Because God’s promises are not information about a distant future; they are the means by which the Spirit unites us to Christ now. When you believe God’s promise that your sins are forgiven, you are freed from guilt and drawn to love him. When you believe that Christ is coming and you will be like him (1 John 3:2–3), you begin to purify yourself as he is pure. A promise believed changes what you want. That is how the new nature grows: not by striving to become divine, but by trusting what God has said, until his character is reproduced in yours.

Having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire. “Escaped” (apophygontes) means fled from, got away from, like a man running out of a burning building. “Corruption” (phthora) is decay, moral rot, the process by which something good goes bad and is destroyed. “Sinful desire” (epithymia) is craving, lust. The world’s rot comes from disordered desire (James 1:14–15). The clause defines the divine nature by its opposite: what is shared is the opposite of corruption. It is a promise of holiness and incorruption, not of divinity. Peter will use the same word in chapter 2 of the false teachers, who promise freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption (2:19). There are only two directions: toward God’s life, or toward the rot.

Where Christians differ: do believers become divine? Eastern Orthodoxy teaches theosis or deification, in which believers progressively become gods by grace. Some modern movements teach that believers become little gods. Verdict: Believers share in God’s moral nature (his holiness, love and life) through union with Christ by the Spirit, but they never share in his essence, his deity, or his incommunicable attributes like omnipotence or omniscience. The Creator-creature distinction is never erased. We become like God in character, not God in being (1 John 3:2; 2 Corinthians 3:18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers become sinless now, or merge into God. It means God’s life is truly in us, transforming us into his likeness.

In a sentence. His divine power has given us everything we need for a godly life through our knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and goodness. Through these he has given us his very great and precious promises, so that through them you may share in the divine nature, having escaped the corruption in the world caused by evil desires.

On a Tuesday. Take one promise of God and carry it through the day. If you are anxious, his promise never to leave you (Hebrews 13:5); if you are tempted, his promise of a way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13); if you are guilty, his promise to forgive the one who confesses (1 John 1:9). When the desire that rots presses on you, answer it with what God has said, and see whether the promise does not prove stronger than the craving. And if you are tempted to go looking for something more than Christ, a newer teaching or a deeper secret, stop and ask what you have not yet used of what he has given.

For worship. God has not given us a starter kit and left us to complete the set. He has given everything, by his own divine power, and the gift remains. He called us by his glory into his glory, and he bound himself with promises so precious and so great that they make sinners share his holy life. We were rotting in the world’s decay, and he brought us out. We were made of dust, and he will not make us gods, but he has made us his children, partakers of the life that has no end. All of it is ours through knowing one Person, our God and Saviour Jesus Christ, in whom nothing is lacking.

verseByVerse.quote: For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge, and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness, and godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge, and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness, and godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love.

For this very reason, make every effort. “For this very reason”: because God has given you everything (vv. 3–4). The effort rests on a gift already complete, which is the New Testament’s invariable order. God’s gift is the basis for our effort, not a replacement for it. “Make every effort” (spoudēn pasan pareisenenkantes) is literally bringing in all diligence alongside, applying all eagerness. God has brought everything; you bring your diligence beside it. Grace calls for strenuous effort (Philippians 2:12–13): work out your salvation, for it is God who works in you. Grace is not opposed to effort; it is opposed to earning. A man who has been given a farm does not earn it by ploughing, but he will certainly plough.

To supplement your faith with virtue. The verb behind “supplement” (epichorēgēsate) is the chorēgos word: in Athens the chorēgos was the wealthy citizen who funded a chorus for the great festivals and paid for everything it needed, lavishly, at his own expense. Peter used the word of God’s supply in his first letter (1 Peter 4:11); here he asks the same generosity from them. Not a grudging minimum but full provision. Then eight qualities in a chain, each growing out of the last. And it starts where it must: faith, which is not one link among others but the ground. On faith seven qualities are built. The first is “virtue” (aretē), moral excellence, goodness, the same word used of God in verse 3. God called us by his excellence, and now his excellence is to appear in us.

And virtue with knowledge. “Knowledge” (gnōsis) here is understanding and practical wisdom: knowing God’s will and how to apply it. It follows virtue because goodness without understanding blunders. Zeal without knowledge has done enormous damage in the church (Romans 10:2). The good man must learn what is good.

And knowledge with self-control. “Self-control” (enkrateia) is self-mastery, literally holding oneself in. It follows knowledge, since knowing what is right settles nothing until the appetites are governed. The false teachers had knowledge, or claimed it, without self-control (2:10–14), and Peter describes where that ends.

And self-control with steadfastness. “Steadfastness” (hypomonē) is endurance, remaining under weight, patience under pressure (James 1:3–4). It is self-control extended over time, which is a different and harder thing. Anyone can resist a temptation once. Steadfastness is resisting it on the four hundredth day, when the novelty of the fight has gone and the pressure has not.

And steadfastness with godliness. “Godliness” (eusebeia) is reverence for God shown in life. It turns the whole sequence God-ward and prevents it becoming mere self-mastery. A Stoic philosopher could have admired the first five qualities. Godliness is what makes them Christian: everything done before God’s face, for his sake.

And godliness with brotherly affection. “Brotherly affection” (philadelphia) is family love for fellow believers: warmth, loyalty, enjoyment of one another, as brothers and sisters who belong to the same Father. Godliness that does not love God’s children is not godliness (1 John 4:20).

And brotherly affection with love. “Love” (agapē) is self-giving love that reaches past the family to everyone, including enemies. It is the crown of the list (1 Corinthians 13:13; Colossians 3:14). The list begins with faith and ends with love. The direction is the thing to see. It runs from what God has given, through the ordering of one’s own character, and out to other people, and it ends at love, the goal the whole chain has been moving toward. The last link is the one that looks most like Christ, who loved his own and also prayed for those who crucified him.

Is this effort not a kind of legalism? No. Legalism is effort to earn God’s favour or to add to Christ’s work. Peter’s effort springs from favour already given: because God has granted you everything, make every effort. The difference is the difference between a slave labouring to buy his freedom and a son working in his father’s fields. Both may sweat. Only one does it from rest. If you notice that your effort has become anxious, proud or joyless, the remedy is not to stop trying but to go back to verses 3–4 and remember what you have been given.

Must I master these qualities one at a time, in order? No. Peter is not describing a staircase where you finish one step before you begin the next. The links grow together, each strengthening the others, like branches on one tree. The order shows how they depend on one another: knowledge guides goodness, self-control keeps knowledge honest, endurance makes self-control last. But a young believer shows something of all of them from the start, and the oldest saint is still growing in every one.

What does adding self-control actually look like? Start with one appetite that rules you more than it should: food, the phone, anger, spending, sleep, lust. Decide in advance, in the light of God’s word, what obedience looks like there. Remove what feeds it where you can. Tell a trusted believer and ask him to ask you. When you fail, confess it at once, receive forgiveness, and go again the same day. Self-control is not gritted teeth alone; it is the Spirit’s fruit (Galatians 5:23), and it grows as you rely on him in specific, repeated choices.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we earn salvation by adding virtues. Faith is the gift that saves; these virtues are the growth of a saved life. Nor does it mean each must be achieved before the next; they grow together.

In a sentence. For this very reason, make every effort to add goodness to your faith; and to goodness, knowledge; and to knowledge, self-control; and to self-control, perseverance; and to perseverance, godliness; and to godliness, love for fellow believers; and to that love, love for all.

On a Tuesday. Which of these seven qualities is weakest in your life? Make a deliberate effort to grow in it this week, relying on God’s power. Be specific: not I will be more loving, but I will visit, phone or help this person, whom I have been avoiding. Not I will be more godly, but I will begin the day with his word before my phone. Ask someone who knows you well which link they see missing; the answer may surprise you.

For worship. Look at the chain and see a portrait. Faith resting wholly on the Father, goodness without a stain, knowledge of the Father’s will so perfect that he did always what pleased him, self-control in the wilderness when he was hungry, steadfastness all the way to the cross, godliness that said not my will but yours, affection for his brothers, and love for his enemies. Every link was first in Christ. And the God who called us by that excellence has promised to reproduce it in us, giving lavishly what he asks us to supply lavishly, until the family likeness is complete.

verseByVerse.quote: For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. For whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. For whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins.

For if these qualities are yours and are increasing. Two conditions, and the second is the interesting one. “Are yours” (hyparchonta) means they belong to you, are present in you. “Increasing” (pleonazonta) means abounding, multiplying. Not merely present but increasing: Peter assumes growth is the normal state, and that a static Christian life is already a warning sign. Living things grow. A tree that has not grown for years is either very old or dead.

They keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. The two negatives are worth separating. “Ineffective” (argous) is literally idle, unemployed; it was used of land lying fallow and of the workers standing idle in the marketplace (Matthew 20:3, 6). “Unfruitful” (akarpous) is barren, without output. Knowledge of Christ is meant to produce fruit (John 15:8; Colossians 1:10). And note the sphere: ineffective in the knowledge of Christ. Peter is not saying these qualities earn knowledge, but that without them a man’s knowing goes nowhere. You may hold the doctrine accurately and be entirely unproductive in it, like a field with the best soil in the county that nobody has sown.

For whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind. The word for nearsighted (myōpazōn, from which comes myopic) means squinting, screwing up the eyes to see something close. It is a wonderfully exact description. The man is not blind to everything: he can see what is right in front of him perfectly well, this week, this appetite, this grievance, this pay rise. What he cannot see is anything at a distance: eternity, the judgement seat, the coming kingdom, the souls of people around him. Spiritual short-sightedness, left alone, becomes blindness (typhlos). And it is the false teachers’ disease exactly. They will scoff at the coming of the Lord (3:4), because they cannot see further than their own desires.

Having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins. And there is the root. “Forgotten” is literally having taken forgetfulness (lēthēn labōn), as though he had picked it up and put it on. “Cleansed” (katharismos) is purification, the word used of Christ’s work when he made purification for sins (Hebrews 1:3). He has lost sight of his own cleansing: not necessarily lost the cleansing, but the memory of it. A Christian who forgets what he was forgiven has no fuel for growth, because gratitude is the engine of the whole chain in verses 5–7. Which suggests where to look when growth has stopped. Not usually at a missing technique, but at a memory that has gone dim. The woman in Luke 7 who washed Jesus’ feet with her tears loved much because she knew she had been forgiven much.

I feel stuck and fruitless. Am I a Christian at all? The fact that it troubles you is a good sign; the man Peter describes is not troubled, he is drowsy. Begin where Peter puts the problem: with memory. Go back to the cross and look again at what your sins cost and how freely they were washed away. Read a Gospel slowly, or Psalm 103, or Isaiah 53. Confess the specific sins that have choked growth. Then take one step of obedience in one of the qualities of verses 5–7. Fruit grows slowly and is often seen first by others, so ask a mature believer what they see. And do not judge your whole standing by one dry season; judge it by where you run.

What it does not mean. It does not necessarily mean such a person was never cleansed; it describes a professing believer who has lost sight of grace. Whether genuine or not will be shown by whether he returns (v. 10).

In a sentence. For if you possess these qualities in increasing measure, they will keep you from being ineffective and unproductive in your knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. But whoever does not have them is short-sighted and blind, forgetting that they have been cleansed from their past sins.

On a Tuesday. Notice what filled your vision today. If almost everything you thought about was within the next week, money, the next meal, an argument, a screen, you are squinting. Lift your eyes deliberately: before you sleep, think about the day you will see Christ, and about one person you know who is without him. And remember one specific sin you have been forgiven. Thank him for it by name. The memory will do more for your growth than a new resolution.

For worship. He made purification for sins, once, by himself, and then sat down. There is no stain he left half-washed, and no former sin he keeps in reserve against his people. If we forget, he does not: he remembers that we are dust, and he remembers our sins no more. And the eyes that are squinting at this world’s small things he will one day open to see him face to face. Until then, the memory of his cleansing is enough to keep a whole life fruitful, because nothing gives such growth as knowing how much you have been forgiven by so great a Saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall. For in this way there will be richly provided for you an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall. For in this way there will be richly provided for you an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent. “Be diligent” (spoudasate, make every effort) echoes verse 5, and “all the more” (mallon) raises it. And notice “brothers”: the only time in the letter Peter addresses his readers so. The warning about the blind man of verse 9 is followed at once by the warmth of family. He is not threatening them from a distance; he is a brother pleading with brothers.

To confirm your calling and election. The sentence has troubled readers, and the trouble dissolves on a careful look at who is being confirmed to whom. “Confirm” (bebaian poieisthai) means to make firm, make sure, establish; it was a legal term for ratifying a contract or guaranteeing a sale. “Calling” (klēsis) is God’s effectual call; “election” (eklogē) is God’s eternal choice. Peter does not say make God’s election secure: that is not in anyone’s power, and this letter grounds everything in what God’s divine power has granted. Election is God’s act and is settled. Calling is mentioned first because it is how we come to know our election: we see the call in time and learn from it the choice made before time. We cannot make our election more certain to God; it is fixed. But we can make it more certain to ourselves, by growing in the qualities of verses 5–7, which are the evidence of genuine faith. The fruit does not create the root; it demonstrates it. That is how the Reformed tradition has always read this: not works establishing salvation, but works establishing certainty.

The kindness in it. There is real pastoral tenderness here. A Christian anxious about whether he is truly God’s is not told to search his memory for a decisive moment, nor to look inward for a feeling. He is told to look for growth in ordinary character, which is visible, and which other people can see too. Election is not a locked room to be broken into by speculation. It is a fact God has made known through his call, and confirmed in lives that are being changed.

For if you practice these qualities you will never fall. “Practise” (poiountes) is present tense: keep doing. “Never fall” (ou mē ptaisēte pote) is a strong double negative: you will certainly never, ever stumble. The verb is used of stumbling, and James uses it of the many ways we all stumble in speech (James 3:2). Here it is not a promise of sinlessness but of not coming to ruin: you will never fall away, never stumble in the decisive sense, never be lost.

Does if you practise these qualities mean that perseverance depends on our effort? The qualities are the fruit of the divine power that has given us all we need (v. 3), and by them believers confirm their calling, show it to be real, to themselves and others. Those who belong to Christ are kept by him (John 10:28–29); diligence is the way his keeping works out in our lives, not a rival to it.

For in this way there will be richly provided for you an entrance into the eternal kingdom. “Richly provided” (plousiōs epichorēgēthēsetai) is the chorēgos word again, as in verse 5, and now the direction reverses. They were told to supply these qualities lavishly; God will lavishly supply their entrance. The generosity given comes back multiplied at the door. “Entrance” (eisodos) is a way in, a welcome: like a victorious athlete or general welcomed home through the city gates with celebration. Not a man scraping in as the door shuts, smelling of smoke (1 Corinthians 3:15), but a son coming home to a feast. “Eternal kingdom”: God’s reign in its fullness, which no false teacher can scoff away.

Of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. The same construction as verse 1: one person, Lord and Saviour. The kingdom is his, and the welcome at its gate is his welcome.

Where Christians differ: can I know I am elect? Some fear election makes assurance impossible: how can I know if God chose me? Others think assurance comes only by special revelation. Verdict: Believers can and should have assurance of their election. It is grounded first in God’s promises in Christ, received by faith; it is confirmed by the Spirit’s inner witness (Romans 8:16) and by the fruit of a godly life (1 John 2:3; 3:14). Election is not a cause for anxiety but for confidence: those who trust Christ and grow in godliness may know they are chosen (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). And the elect will persevere: they will never fall.

Can a true Christian fall away and be lost? No. Those God has chosen and called he keeps, and none of them will be snatched out of Christ’s hand (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:30; Philippians 1:6). True believers can fall into serious sin for a time, as Peter himself did on the night he denied the Lord, and they may lose the joy of their salvation and come under the Father’s discipline. But they are brought back, because Christ prays for them as he prayed for Peter (Luke 22:32). Those who abandon the faith altogether show that they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). So the promise of this verse is not a reason to relax but a reason to keep going without fear.

What if I look and cannot see the fruit? First, look at Christ before you look at yourself. Assurance rests first on his promise to receive all who come (John 6:37), not on your inspection. Second, look honestly but not morbidly: fruit is often small, slow and more visible to others than to you. Do you trust him? Do you want to obey him? Do you grieve over sin? Do you love his people? Third, if you find almost nothing, do not sit down in despair. Go to Christ now as a sinner, and begin to obey. The way to confirm your calling is not endless self-examination but present faith and diligence.

What it does not mean. It does not mean our good works cause our election or our entrance into the kingdom. They confirm it. The kingdom is given by grace.

In a sentence. Therefore, my brothers and sisters, make every effort to confirm your calling and election. For if you do these things, you will never stumble, and you will receive a rich welcome into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Instead of asking am I elect? in the abstract, ask what God’s call has done in you this year. Write down two ways you have grown and one way you need to. Thank God for the first, because it is his work; give diligence to the second. And when you are tempted to coast, remember the welcome at the end: you are not working to get through the door, you are living now as someone who is expected at a feast.

For worship. Before the world was made he chose us, and in time his voice found us and called us by name. He keeps those he calls, so that the one who stumbled on a dark night by a courtyard fire could write, thirty years later, you will never fall. And at the end there is not a narrow gate grudgingly opened but an entrance richly supplied, the generous God of the chorus pouring out everything for the homecoming of his children into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. The election was his, the calling was his, the keeping is his, and the welcome will be his.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — Eyewitnesses and the Prophetic Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter knows he will soon die, as Jesus told him, so he keeps reminding them of what they already know. Their faith does not rest on clever myths: the apostles saw Christ’s majesty and heard the Father’s voice on the mountain. And they have the prophetic word, confirmed by that event, a lamp in a dark place until the day dawns. No prophecy came from the prophet’s own understanding; men spoke from God as the Holy Spirit carried them along.
verseByVerse.theology:
Carried Along

Prophecy did not come from the prophet's own interpretation. Men spoke from God as the Holy Spirit carried them along — fully human, and fully God's word.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter wrote knowing his death was near, and arranged for his readers to remember.

Now: Scripture is a lamp in a dark place — enough light until the day dawns.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I intend always to remind you of these qualities, though you know them and are established in the truth that you have. I think it right, as long as I am in this body, to stir you up by way of reminder, since I know that the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me. And I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I intend always to remind you of these qualities, though you know them and are established in the truth that you have. I think it right, as long as I am in this body, to stir you up by way of reminder, since I know that the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me. And I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things.

Therefore I intend always to remind you of these qualities. “Remind” (hypomimnēskein) means keep reminding, and it is a key theme of the letter (1:12, 13, 15; 3:1–2). Peter is not correcting ignorance. He says plainly that they know these things and are established in them, and he intends to go on saying them anyway. That is a considered view of what teaching is for, and it cuts against the appetite for novelty that the false teachers were exploiting. Believers do not chiefly need new truth; they need to remember old truth. Most of what a congregation needs is not new information but the same truth said again, because knowing a thing and having it present to you are different states. A man knows he loves his wife; he still needs to remember it at six o’clock on a tiring evening.

Though you know them and are established in the truth that you have. “Established” (estērigmenous) means made firm, and it is perfect tense: settled and still standing. It is the word Jesus used to Peter on the night of the denial: when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers (Luke 22:32). Thirty years later the old apostle is doing exactly that. The man who could not stand firm for a night is spending his last days making others firm.

I think it right, as long as I am in this body, to stir you up by way of reminder. “Body” (skēnōma) is literally tent, tabernacle, and the image governs the paragraph. A tent is temporary accommodation, struck when the journey moves on (2 Corinthians 5:1–4). The body is not the person; it is the dwelling he lives in for a while. And “stir you up” (diegeirein) means to wake someone, to arouse, to keep awake. It is used of the disciples waking Jesus in the storm (Luke 8:24), and Peter uses it again in 3:1. His model of ministry is not filling empty heads but waking drowsy ones. Perhaps he remembered Gethsemane, where three times he slept while his Lord prayed. He knows how easily disciples doze.

Is it not boring to hear the same things again and again? Only if you think the purpose of hearing is to collect information. Food is the same every day and nobody calls bread boring; we need it again because we used up the last meal. The gospel is like that. Yesterday’s assurance does not carry today’s temptation; the truth must be brought fresh to a heart that leaks. A good preacher will find new ways to say old things, but you should be suspicious of any teacher whose main selling point is that he has something nobody has heard before. In Christian truth, what is new is seldom true, and what is true is never stale to a hungry soul.

Since I know that the putting off of my body will be soon. “Putting off” (apothesis) is laying aside, as one takes off clothing or strikes a tent. Death is a laying aside of the body, not the end of the person. Peter speaks of it calmly, the way a traveller speaks of folding up his tent before setting out on the last stage of a journey.

As our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me. Peter knows he is going to die, and he knows it because he was told. On the beach, after the third question about love, Jesus said that when he was old others would stretch out his hands and lead him where he did not want to go, and John adds that this indicated the kind of death by which he would glorify God (John 21:18–19). It pointed to crucifixion. Tradition says Peter was crucified upside down in Rome under Nero, at his own request, feeling unworthy to die as his Lord had. So this letter is written by a man under a sentence he has been carrying for thirty years. He was told it on the morning of his restoration, in the same conversation in which Jesus said, follow me. And he has been following ever since, toward that death, with his eyes open.

And I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things. “Departure” (exodos) is exodus, going out, the word Moses and Elijah used on the mountain of Jesus’ own death, his departure which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). Peter had heard that word spoken on the holy mountain, and now uses it of himself. His death is an exodus: a going out of bondage, through the sea, into the promised land, behind the Lord who went first. And what he does with the knowledge is the striking thing. He is not settling affairs or saying farewells. He is arranging for them to remember after he has gone, which is very likely why we have this letter at all. “Recall” is literally to make memory. Perhaps through this letter, or through Mark’s Gospel, which early tradition says records Peter’s preaching.

How should a Christian think about his own death? As Peter did: as the folding of a tent and an exodus, not as the end. To be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), at once, not in a sleep and not in a purgatory, but with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). We may still fear dying, the process, the pain, the parting, and that is no sin; even Jesus was in anguish in the garden. But death itself has lost its sting (1 Corinthians 15:55–57). So use the time well. Peter’s question was not how long have I left? but what will they remember when I am gone? Ask the same.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Peter feared death. He speaks of it calmly as a departure. Nor does it mean believers can do without reminders; even the established need them.

In a sentence. So I will always remind you of these things, even though you know them and are firmly established in the truth you now have. I think it is right to refresh your memory as long as I live in the tent of this body, because I know that I will soon put it aside, as our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me. And I will make every effort to see that after my departure you will always be able to remember these things.

On a Tuesday. Think about what spiritual legacy you will leave behind. Not money or property, but the truth you will have planted in other people. Who will remember Christ better because of you: your children, a younger believer, a friend? Write a short letter this week to one of them, telling them what Christ has been to you. You need not be dying to do it. And thank God, by name, for one person who kept reminding you of the gospel when you already knew it.

For worship. The Lord who told Peter how he would die also told him to follow, and walked ahead of him into death and out of it. Jesus accomplished his exodus at Jerusalem, so that the exodus of every believer is safe: a tent folded, a door opened, a servant at home with his Master. He strengthened the man who failed him, and then used him to strengthen his brothers for two thousand years. Our Lord does not forget his people’s weakness, and he does not waste it. He wakes the drowsy, he reminds the forgetful, and he brings every one of his pilgrims home.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus had told Peter how he would die.

verseByVerse.quote: For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. For when he received honor and glory from God the Father, and the voice was borne to him by the Majestic Glory, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased," we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. For when he received honor and glory from God the Father, and the voice was borne to him by the Majestic Glory, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased,” we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain.

For we did not follow cleverly devised myths. The charge is answered head-on. “Cleverly devised” (sesophismenois) means sophisticated, cunningly crafted, made up; “myths” (mythois) are fables, legends. The false teachers were evidently saying that the promised coming of Christ was a story, the kind of tale religious men tell to frighten people into good behaviour. And Peter’s reply is not philosophical but historical. The ancient world was full of myths: gods who came down, died and rose with the seasons, stories that never claimed to have happened at any particular place or time. The gospel is not like that. It names a governor, a city, a mountain, and men who were there. It is history, not myth.

When we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. “Power and coming” (dynamin kai parousian) probably means his powerful coming: the second coming, which the false teachers denied (3:4). “Coming” (parousia) was used of the arrival of a king on a state visit. Peter’s point is that the apostles did not invent the return of Christ. They had already seen a preview of it.

But we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. The word for eyewitnesses is epoptai, and it was used in the mystery religions for those admitted to the highest grade of initiation: those who had seen. Peter takes the vocabulary of the cults his opponents traded in and applies it to something that happened on a mountain in daylight before three fishermen. “Majesty” (megaleiotēs) is greatness, magnificence, the word used when the crowds were astonished at the majesty of God in Jesus’ healing (Luke 9:43). At the Transfiguration, Peter saw a preview of Christ’s coming glory: the King’s face as it will be seen on the day he comes.

For when he received honor and glory from God the Father. Peter is describing the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1–8; Mark 9:2–8; Luke 9:28–36), and he was one of three men there. Jesus’ face shone like the sun, his clothes became dazzling white, and Moses and Elijah appeared and spoke with him. Honour and glory were given him by the Father, the honour of the Father’s word and the glory of his own radiance shining through.

And the voice was borne to him by the Majestic Glory. “Majestic Glory” (megaloprepous doxēs, magnificent glory) is a reverent way of naming God, perhaps referring to the bright cloud of God’s presence that overshadowed them. It is the cloud that filled the tabernacle and the temple, the glory that Moses asked to see. On the mountain it came down again.

This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased. The Father’s declaration (Matthew 17:5), echoing Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1, and the words at Jesus’ baptism (Matthew 3:17). Notice what Peter selects. He does not describe the shining face or the white clothes or Moses and Elijah. He reports the voice, because the argument concerns testimony, and what settles the matter is not what he saw but what was said. The Father himself named his Son, King and Servant, and declared his delight in him.

We ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain. “We ourselves”: Peter, James and John. The emphasis is on hearing, twice, and on presence. The holy mountain is the Mount of Transfiguration, where Peter, James and John saw Jesus glorified, made holy by God’s presence as Sinai once was; tradition suggests Mount Tabor, though Mount Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi, fits the Gospel accounts well. Peter’s testimony is firsthand. And there is something moving in the restraint. Peter had wanted to build three shelters and stay, and had spoken without knowing what he was saying (Luke 9:33). He mentions none of that. Thirty-odd years on he reports only what is admissible: we were there, and we heard.

Why does the Transfiguration prove that Christ will come again? Because it was the coming in miniature. Jesus had just said that some standing there would not taste death until they saw the Son of Man coming in his kingdom (Matthew 16:28), and six days later three of them did: the glory he will have when he comes was briefly uncovered before their eyes. The scoffers said the King would never come in power. Peter replies that he has already seen the King in his power. What was hidden for a moment on the mountain will be revealed to the whole world on the last day.

How do we know the apostles were not simply mistaken or lying? Consider what their testimony cost them. Men do not willingly die for what they know to be a lie, and Peter is writing under the shadow of crucifixion. Their accounts are sober, full of their own failures, written within living memory of the events, when others who were there could contradict them. And the testimony is not one man’s vision: three men on the mountain, and hundreds who saw the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 15:6). Christian faith is not a leap in the dark; it is trust in reliable witnesses, confirmed by the Spirit who opens our eyes to see that what they say is true.

Should I seek experiences of glory like Peter’s? No. Peter himself, having had the greatest experience a man could have, does not tell his readers to seek one. He points them in the next verse to the prophetic word. The Transfiguration was a unique moment given to chosen witnesses to found the church’s testimony, and it has been written down so that you may believe without seeing (John 20:29). God may give believers deep joy and a sense of his nearness, and we may thank him for it, but our faith rests on what happened and what is written, not on what we feel.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christian faith rests on experiences of glory. Peter will say the prophetic word is even more sure (v. 19). It means the gospel rests on real, historical events witnessed by reliable people.

In a sentence. For when we told you about the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ in power, we were not following cleverly made-up stories, but we had seen his majesty with our own eyes. He received honour and glory from God the Father when the voice came to him from the Majestic Glory, saying, “This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased.” We ourselves heard this voice that came from heaven when we were with him on the sacred mountain.

On a Tuesday. When someone dismisses the faith as a nice story, do not be rattled and do not be defensive. Say plainly that Christianity stands or falls on events, a death and a resurrection witnessed by named men, and offer to read one of the Gospels with them. And when your own faith feels thin, go back to the facts rather than to your feelings: he lived, he died, he rose, he was seen, and the Father has spoken about him.

For worship. On the holy mountain the curtain was drawn back for a moment, and the carpenter of Nazareth stood in the glory that was his before the world existed. The cloud that once filled the temple came down, and the Father spoke of his Son with delight. That is the Lord we follow: not a myth or a moral idea but the beloved Son, whose face shone like the sun, who came down the mountain to go to a cross, and who will come again in the same majesty, no longer hidden from anyone. The Father is well pleased with him. And because we are in him, the Father is well pleased with us too.
verseByVerse.note: The “holy mountain” is the Mount of Transfiguration, where Peter, James and John saw Jesus’ glory.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts,

And we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed. “Prophetic word” (ton prophētikon logon) is the Old Testament Scriptures as a whole, which prophesy Christ, including his coming in glory. “More fully confirmed” (bebaioteron) means more sure, more firm, more reliable; it is from the same family as the word for confirming your calling (v. 10). There are two readings. First, the Transfiguration confirmed the prophecies, making them even more certain to us: the voice on the mountain and the writings agree. Second, the prophetic Scriptures are even more reliable than Peter’s experience. The second fits well with verses 20–21: Scripture is more certain than any experience, even an apostle’s vision, because it comes from God himself. Either way Peter is not belittling what he saw; he has just staked his case on being an eyewitness. And either way his readers, who were not on the mountain and never would be, are told that what they hold in their hands is the firmest ground there is. That is a considerable dignity to give a book.

Is Scripture really more certain than seeing something with my own eyes? Yes, in this sense: eyes can be deceived, memories fade, and experiences need interpreting, but God’s written word does not change and cannot lie. Peter’s experience on the mountain was real, yet it lasted minutes, was seen by three men, and needed words from God to explain it. Scripture is God’s own permanent testimony, given for every believer in every age. So when an experience, a dream, an impression or a strong feeling seems to say one thing and Scripture says another, Scripture wins every time. That is not distrust of God’s work in us; it is trust in his clearest word to us.

To which you will do well to pay attention. “Pay attention” (prosechontes) means give heed to, hold the mind on, as a sailor holds his eye on a light. And “you will do well” is gentle: not a threat but an encouragement, the way a guide might say you will do well to keep close to the lamp.

As to a lamp shining in a dark place. The image is exactly weighted. “Lamp” (lychnos) is a small oil lamp. “Dark place” (auchmēros topos) means a dry, dirty, murky place, squalid, the kind of corner where nothing grows and nobody would choose to stay. This world, darkened by sin and false teaching, is like a dark, squalid room, and Scripture is the lamp that shows the way (Psalm 119:105). A lamp is not the sun; it is enough to see the next few feet by, and it is indispensable if the alternative is total darkness. Peter is honest about how much light Scripture gives in this age: sufficient, and not yet daylight. We do not see everything. We see enough to walk.

Until the day dawns. “Day dawns” (hēmera diaugasē) is literally shines through: the day of Christ’s return (Romans 13:12), when the night of this age is over. The lamp is temporary. There is a morning coming, and when it arrives nobody will need a lamp.

And the morning star rises in your hearts. “Morning star” (phōsphoros, light-bearer) is the planet Venus, the last light before sunrise and the herald of it. It points to Christ himself, the bright morning star (Revelation 22:16), the star that would come out of Jacob (Numbers 24:17), the sun of righteousness who rises with healing in his wings (Malachi 4:2). So the dawn is his coming, which is precisely what the false teachers were denying. “In your hearts” is the phrase that surprises. Peter has been arguing about history and testimony, and lands on the inward. When Christ returns, believers will know him fully, with full inner illumination (1 Corinthians 13:12). The same Christ who will appear publicly is the one who will fill the heart with light. Until then, we need the lamp of Scripture.

Does God still speak today apart from the Bible? This app holds that the gifts of new revelation, prophecy in the sense of authoritative words from God, ceased with the apostles, and that the canon of Scripture is closed (Hebrews 1:1–2; Jude 3). Many dear brothers in Christ believe otherwise, and we hold our view with charity. But on the practical point there is wide agreement among Bible-believing Christians: Scripture is the lamp, sufficient for faith and life, and nothing that claims to be from God may add to it or contradict it. The Spirit does speak today, through the word he inspired, applying it to our hearts. If you want to hear God speak, open the Bible.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Scripture is unnecessary once we have a personal experience of Christ. We need it until he returns. Nor does dark place mean Scripture is dim; it is a bright lamp in a dark world.

In a sentence. We also have the prophetic message as something even more reliable, and you will do well to pay attention to it, as to a light shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts.

On a Tuesday. Treat the Bible today as a lamp, not an ornament. Before a decision, a hard conversation or a temptation, read a passage and hold your mind on it. Keep a verse with you for the dark corners of the day. And if you have let the lamp gather dust, light it again tonight: start with a Gospel, read a chapter, and ask the Lord to show you himself in it.

For worship. God has not left us in the dark. He lit a lamp and put it in our hands, and every page of it was shining toward one Person. The prophets saw his star rising from far off; the apostles saw his glory on the mountain; and we hold their word, more sure than any vision. And the night will not last for ever. The morning star is already rising. One day the lamp will be set down, not because it failed, but because the Sun himself has come, and we shall see him whom we have loved without seeing, and our hearts will be full of his light.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation. For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone’s own interpretation. For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.

Knowing this first of all. “First of all” (prōton) means above all, of first importance. Before anything else about Scripture, know where it came from.

That no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone’s own interpretation. The verse is quoted in two directions, and the context settles it. “Interpretation” (epilysis) means explanation, unravelling, solution, the untying of a knot. It is often taken to mean that no individual may interpret Scripture privately. That may be a reasonable caution, but it is not what Peter is arguing here. The subject throughout is the origin of prophecy, not its later handling, and verse 21 explains verse 20 directly, beginning with for. The sense is that prophecy did not arise from the prophet’s own reading of things. It was not a gifted man’s insight into his times, however inspired we might loosely call that. Prophets did not make up their messages based on their own insight into events. It came from outside them.

For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man. “Produced” (ēnechthē) means was brought, was carried. The negative is absolute: ever. And the will of man covers both intention and capacity. Scripture did not begin with human initiative or decision. No prophet sat down and decided to write the word of God.

But men spoke from God. Two things held together, and the New Testament’s doctrine of Scripture lives in the combination. Men spoke: real people, with their own vocabulary, style and circumstances. Isaiah does not sound like Amos; Paul does not sound like John. And they spoke “from God” (apo theou): God was the source. Human authors truly spoke, using their own languages, styles and personalities, but the message originated with God.

As they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. That verb (pheromenoi, borne along, driven) is a sailing word. It is used in Acts 27:15 and 17 of Paul’s ship, which had lost the power to steer and was driven before the wind: the sailors gave way to it and were carried along. And it is the same verb Peter used twice in verses 17–18 of the voice borne from heaven. The voice was carried to the mountain; the prophets were carried by the Spirit. The men are not passive cargo; they are working the vessel, raising the sails. But the Spirit supplied the power and direction, and they arrived where the wind took them. This is the doctrine of inspiration: Scripture is God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16), fully human and fully divine in its authorship, so that what Scripture says, God says. Which is why the Bible reads as both thoroughly human and entirely God’s word, and why Peter can appeal to it against men who were rewriting the future to suit themselves.

Where Christians differ: is Scripture fully inspired and without error? Some hold that Scripture is inspired only in its religious teaching, or that it contains human errors alongside divine truth. Verdict: Because Scripture came from God through men carried along by the Spirit, it shares God’s truthfulness. It is inerrant in all that it affirms, infallible in its teaching, and sufficient for faith and life. The human authors were not mere typewriters; God used their personalities and research (Luke 1:1–4). But the Spirit so guided them that what they wrote is the very word of God (1 Thessalonians 2:13). Sola Scriptura: Scripture is the final authority over every tradition, experience and claim of revelation.

Does this mean that individual Christians may not interpret Scripture for themselves? Roman Catholic teaching has used the verse to argue that the church alone can interpret Scripture rightly. But Peter is speaking of where prophecy came from: not from the prophet’s own understanding, but from God, as men were carried along by the Spirit (v. 21). Every believer is to read and understand Scripture (Acts 17:11), humbly, in the fellowship of the church and with its teachers, testing all interpretation by Scripture itself.

Does this apply to the New Testament too? Yes. Peter speaks here of Old Testament prophecy, but in 3:2 he puts the commandment of the apostles alongside the prophets, and in 3:15–16 he places Paul’s letters among the other Scriptures. The same Spirit who carried the prophets was promised to the apostles to bring to their remembrance all that Jesus said and to guide them into all the truth (John 14:26; 16:13). The church did not make these books Scripture; it recognised the voice of its Shepherd in them. With the apostles’ writings the canon is complete, and no further book will be added (Jude 3; Hebrews 1:1–2).

What about the parts of the Bible that seem to contradict each other or science? Take them seriously, but humbly. Many apparent contradictions dissolve when we read carefully: different writers choosing different details, round numbers, the way ancient historians summarised speeches, or ordinary language describing what the eye sees, as we still say the sun rises. Some difficulties remain unsolved, and good Christian scholars have honestly said so. But a difficulty is not an error, and a great many supposed errors of a century ago have since been answered. When you meet one, keep reading, ask a mature teacher, consult a good commentary, and trust the God who cannot lie (Titus 1:2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean ordinary believers cannot interpret Scripture. They can and should, carefully and humbly, within the fellowship of the church (Acts 17:11). It means no prophet made up the message himself, and no interpreter may twist Scripture to say what he wants (3:16).

In a sentence. Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture came about through the prophet’s own interpretation of things. For prophecy never had its origin in human will, but prophets, though human, spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Read Scripture today as God speaking. Before you open it, ask the Spirit who carried its writers to open your eyes. Read a passage in its context, ask what it meant to its first hearers, and then what it says to you. When you hear a teacher claim the Bible says something surprising, do what the Bereans did and check (Acts 17:11). And when the word rebukes you, do not argue with the wind; set your sails by it.

For worship. The God who made the wind breathed out his word. Across fifteen centuries, through shepherds and kings, prophets and fishermen, in palaces and in exile, the Spirit carried men along until they spoke from God, and every word they wrote is true. He did not leave us to guess at him or to lean on our own understanding. He spoke, and he spoke of his Son. And the same Spirit who carried the prophets now carries their word into our hearts, so that we hear in a book written long ago the living voice of our God, and confess that his word is truth (John 17:17), sweeter than honey to those who love him (Psalm 19:10).

1.theology:
The chapter's great theological claim is 'partakers of the divine nature' (v. 4). This is not deification in the Orthodox sense (we do not become God or merge into the divine essence) nor pantheism (we do not become part of God). It is moral participation: through the Spirit and through union with Christ, God's own character — his holiness, patience, love, truthfulness — is communicated to the believer. Calvin read it as a sharing in God's qualities, not in his essence. The Reformed doctrine of sanctification is nothing less than the outworking of this participation: the divine nature expressing itself in human virtue.

The doctrine of Scripture (vv. 20–21) is equally central. Scripture is not a human document about God; it is God's own word spoken through human instruments. The Spirit carried the prophets; therefore the prophets' words carry divine authority. This is why Peter can call the prophetic word 'more fully confirmed' — the written word outlasts the eyewitness, is available to all, and carries the authority not of human testimony but of the Spirit who inspired it.
1.examples:
The virtue chain (vv. 5–7) addresses a perennial pastoral problem: Christians who park at faith and see no need to move. 'I believe — isn't that enough?' Peter's answer: faith is the beginning, not the destination. A Christian who has been given the divine nature and is not building virtue, knowledge, and love is like a person given a magnificent musical instrument who never practices. The gift is real; the neglect is also real; and the result is the same — no music. Note that Peter does not make the virtues the condition of salvation (they flow from faith, not to it) but the evidence of its reality and the trajectory of its growth.

The lamp-and-morning-star image (v. 19) is a pastoral gift for believers who feel that Scripture reading is dry and unproductive. You do not read the Bible because it is always exciting; you read it because you are in a dark place and it is the only lamp available. The darkness is not a reason to put the lamp down. The lamp is precisely what a dark place requires.

2.title: The Anatomy of a False Teacher
2.text: <sup>1</sup>But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction.<sup>2</sup>And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed.<sup>3</sup>And in their greed they will exploit you with false words.
