Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.<sup>4</sup>For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment;<sup>5</sup>if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly;<sup>6</sup>if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;<sup>7</sup>and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked<sup>8</sup>(for as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard);<sup>9</sup>then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment,<sup>10</sup>and especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority. Bold and willful, they do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones,<sup>11</sup>whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord.<sup>12</sup>But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destruction,<sup>13</sup>suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you.<sup>14</sup>They have eyes full of adultery, insatiable for sin. They entice unsteady souls. They have hearts trained in greed. Accursed children!<sup>15</sup>Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor, who loved gain from wrongdoing,<sup>16</sup>but was rebuked for his own transgression; a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet's madness.<sup>17</sup>These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved.<sup>18</sup>For, speaking loud boasts of folly, they entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error.<sup>19</sup>They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption. For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.<sup>20</sup>For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first.<sup>21</sup>For it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them.<sup>22</sup>What the true proverb says has happened to them: "The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire."
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is Peter’s portrait of the false teacher: his method (slipping in quietly), his doctrine (denying the Master), his motive (greed) and his end (judgment already on its way). Three examples from history, the angels, the flood and Sodom, show that God judges the wicked and rescues the godly. Then Peter describes the teachers themselves: arrogant, driven by appetite, greedy like Balaam, preying on new believers.

The key irony is v. 19: they promise freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption. The test of a teacher is not the sophistication of his words but the shape of his life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Arrival and Judgment of False Teachers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: False prophets troubled Israel, and false teachers will trouble the church. They bring in destructive heresies, deny the Master who bought them, and exploit people for money. But history shows how God acts: he did not spare the angels who sinned, the ancient world, or Sodom, yet he preserved Noah and rescued Lot. So the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and to hold the wicked for judgment.
verseByVerse.theology:
Righteous Lot

False teachers arise from within. God did not spare the angels, the ancient world or Sodom — yet he preserved Noah and rescued Lot. He knows how to rescue the godly and to hold the unrighteous for judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Lot, compromised as he was, was tormented by the evil he saw day after day.

Now: Being grieved by the world’s evil is a mark of the righteous; being comfortable with it is the danger.

verseByVerse.quote: But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction. And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction. And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.

Meaning first. 2 Peter 2 is a sustained warning against false teachers. As there were false prophets in Israel, so there will be false teachers in the church, who secretly introduce destructive heresies, deny the Master who bought them, lead many into immorality, bring the truth into disrepute, and exploit believers out of greed; their judgement is certain (vv. 1–3). Peter proves it from three examples of past judgement: the angels who sinned, the world of Noah’s day, and Sodom and Gomorrah; and two examples of rescue: Noah and Lot. So the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and to hold the unrighteous for judgement (vv. 4–9). The false teachers are then described in vivid detail: they indulge corrupt desires, despise authority, slander heavenly beings, behave like irrational animals, revel in pleasure, have eyes full of adultery, entice the unstable, and are trained in greed; they follow Balaam, who loved the wages of wrongdoing (vv. 10–16). They are waterless springs and mists driven by storms, promising freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption (vv. 17–19). Having once escaped the world’s defilements through knowing Christ, they have been entangled again; their last state is worse than the first, like a dog returning to its vomit or a washed pig returning to the mud (vv. 20–22). It is a dark chapter, but its darkness has a purpose: the Shepherd is showing his flock what the wolves look like, and in the middle of it he tells them that he knows how to rescue his own.

The setting. Much of this chapter closely parallels the letter of Jude, which may have drawn on 2 Peter or vice versa, or both may have used common material. The false teachers seem to have combined a denial of Christ’s return and future judgement (3:3–4) with moral licence: since there is no judgement coming, live as you please. They may have twisted Paul’s teaching on grace into permission to sin (3:15–16). Peter has just spoken of the true prophets, carried along by the Spirit (1:21). Now he turns to the counterfeit, and the hinge is the word but.

But false prophets also arose among the people. “False prophets” (pseudoprophētai): in Israel’s history many claimed to speak for God but did not (Deuteronomy 13:1–5; 18:20–22; Jeremiah 23:9–40). Every true prophet had his shadow. Moses had Balaam, Elijah had the prophets of Baal, Micaiah had four hundred court prophets promising the king victory, Jeremiah had Hananiah breaking the yoke and saying peace, peace, when there was no peace. The parallel is the argument. Israel had them; the church will have them. Peter offers the pattern as a warning rather than a novelty: nobody should be surprised.

Just as there will be false teachers among you. “False teachers” (pseudodidaskaloi). And note among, twice: among the people, among you. Inside the church, not outside (Acts 20:29–30; Matthew 7:15). Not attacking from outside but arising from within, which is what makes them dangerous and hard to name. The greatest danger often comes from within. A persecutor is easy to recognise. A false teacher sits in the next pew, sings the same hymns, and uses the same vocabulary.

Who will secretly bring in destructive heresies. “Secretly bring in” (pareisaxousin) means to smuggle in, to slip in alongside. Nothing is announced; it is introduced quietly next to what is already there. Error rarely arrives as a replacement for the truth. It arrives as an addition, placed beside it, until one day the truth has been edged out of the room. “Destructive” (apōleias) is of destruction, perdition. “Heresies” (haireseis) originally meant choices, then factions or sects, and later false teachings that destroy the faith: a man’s own preference set up against what was delivered.

Even denying the Master who bought them. “Denying” (arnoumenoi) is disowning, renouncing, by their teaching and their lives (Titus 1:16; Jude 4). The word is painful on Peter’s lips: it is the word used of his own three denials in the courtyard. He knows what it is to deny the Lord, and what it is to be brought back. These men deny him and have no tears. “Master” (despotēs) is sovereign lord, the owner of slaves. “Bought” (agorasanta) is the slave-market word: purchased. It is the language of redemption (1 Corinthians 6:20; Revelation 5:9). The picture is of purchased slaves repudiating the man who paid for them, which is the offence he wants felt.

Bringing upon themselves swift destruction. “Swift” (tachinē) is quick, sudden. Their destruction will come suddenly, and it is self-inflicted: they bring it upon themselves.

Where Christians differ: does “the Master who bought them” prove Christ died for everyone, including those who perish? Arminians and some others cite this verse to argue that Christ paid for the sins of all, including false teachers who are finally lost. Verdict: Several points apply. The word is Master (despotēs), not Saviour or Redeemer; it pictures a slave-owner who has purchased slaves, and the false teachers deny his rightful ownership. Peter may be speaking of their own profession: they claimed to be bought by Christ and part of the church, and Peter describes them according to that profession, as one might speak of a church member. Or he may be echoing Deuteronomy 32:6, where Israel as a nation is said to have been bought by God, though many Israelites were not saved. The verse does not use the language of effective redemption from sin (as in 1 Peter 1:18–19). Scripture elsewhere teaches that Christ laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:11, 15), that his death actually secures the salvation of those for whom he died (Romans 8:32–34; Hebrews 10:14), and that the sheep are never lost (John 10:28). The best reading is that the false teachers professed to belong to the Master who purchased the church, and their denial exposed that profession as false.

Were these men ever saved? The chapter suggests not. They returned to their old ways like a dog to its vomit (v. 22), showing that their nature had never changed. They stood within the covenant community and enjoyed everything that came with it: the preaching, the fellowship, the table, the outward cleansing of a changed reputation. And they turned on the One who purchased the church. Peter is not writing a treatise on the extent of the atonement; he is using the language of ownership to make the ingratitude vivid. The lesson for us is not to puzzle over their secret state but to examine our own: do I merely belong to a church that Christ bought, or do I belong to Christ?

And many will follow their sensuality. “Sensuality” (aselgeia) is unrestrained immorality, shameless excess. And notice: many. False teaching is popular, because it usually offers what the flesh already wants. False teaching usually leads to false living, and false living looks for teaching that will excuse it.

And because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. The way of truth is Christianity, the way (Acts 9:2). “Blasphemed” (blasphēmēthēsetai) is slandered. That is the real damage, and it is not primarily to those who are deceived. The gospel’s reputation suffers. Outsiders judge the way of truth by the people carrying its name (Romans 2:24), and this letter’s readers were already being slandered (1 Peter 2:12).

And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. “Greed” (pleonexia) is covetousness, the craving for more. The motive is money, as it was in 1 Timothy 6:5. “Exploit” (emporeusontai) is a trading word, from which comes emporium: they will make merchandise of you. The congregation is the commodity. “False words” (plastois logois) are fabricated, moulded words, from which comes plastic: words shaped to sell rather than to tell the truth.

Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep. “From long ago” (ekpalai): God has long since pronounced judgement on such people (Jude 4). “Not idle” (ouk argei): not lazy, not inactive, the same root as the ineffective Christian of 1:8. “Not asleep” (ou nystazei): not dozing, the word used of the wise and foolish virgins who all grew drowsy (Matthew 25:5). Both images personify judgement as something awake and moving. It has been on its way for a long time and has not stopped. Judgement may seem delayed, but it is wide awake and on its way.

How can I tell a false teacher from a true one who makes mistakes? Look at three things Peter names. First, what he does with Christ: does he deny the Master, his deity, his lordship, his atoning death, his return, or does he exalt him? Second, his life: is his teaching producing holiness or licence, in him and in those who follow him? Third, his motive: is he serving the flock or using it, for money, power or admiration? A sincere teacher may be wrong on secondary matters and still love Christ, live humbly and feed the sheep. Treat him as a brother. A teacher who denies Christ, excuses sin and enriches himself is what this chapter describes, however gifted.

What should I do if I suspect false teaching in my church? Do not gossip and do not panic. First test what is taught by Scripture, carefully and fairly (Acts 17:11; 1 John 4:1). If you are still concerned, speak privately to the person, or to your elders, who are charged with guarding the flock (Acts 20:28–31; Titus 1:9). Be specific about what was said and why it troubles you. If the elders themselves are teaching what denies the gospel and will not be corrected, you may need to leave for a faithful church, quietly and without bitterness. Pray for those being misled, and keep your own heart close to Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every theological disagreement is a destructive heresy. Peter is speaking of denying Christ, combined with immoral living and greed.

In a sentence. But there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you. They will secretly introduce destructive heresies, even denying the sovereign Lord who bought them, bringing swift destruction on themselves. Many will follow their depraved conduct and will bring the way of truth into disrepute. In their greed these teachers will exploit you with stories they have made up. Their condemnation has long been hanging over them, and their destruction has not been sleeping.

On a Tuesday. Watch for teaching that slips in quietly and leads to immorality or greed. Test every teacher by Scripture and by the fruit of their lives. That includes the teachers you listen to online and the books on your nightstand. Ask of each one: does this make Christ greater to me, and make me holier and more generous, or does it make me more comfortable with myself?

For worship. The Master has bought his church. He paid for it with his own blood, and no false teacher can take from him what he purchased. He saw the wolves before they came, and he warned his flock through the mouth of a man who had once denied him and been restored. His judgement on the deceivers is awake, and his care for his sheep is awake too: he who keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps. The way of truth may be slandered for a time, but it is still the way, and it still leads home, because it is Christ himself.
verseByVerse.note: Much of this chapter closely parallels the letter of Jude.

verseByVerse.quote: For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment; if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly; if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment; if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly; if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;

For if God did not spare angels when they sinned. Peter now argues from history, and the sentence is a single long conditional running from verse 4 to verse 9: if, if, if, then. Three examples of judgement, and woven among them, two of rescue. Each supplies something. “Did not spare” (ouk epheisato) is the verb Paul uses of God not sparing his own Son (Romans 8:32), and it is worth holding the two together. God did not spare the angels who sinned, because they deserved judgement. He did not spare his Son, who did not, so that he might spare us. The first case is the highest of creatures. If rank protected anybody it would have protected them, and it did not.

But cast them into hell. “Hell” here is Tartarus (tartarōsas, having cast into Tartarus), used only here in the New Testament: a term from Greek thought for the deepest place of confinement, lower than Hades. Peter borrows a term his readers would understand, the way he borrowed the mystery-cult word for eyewitnesses in 1:16, for the place of confinement of fallen angels.

And committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment. “Chains” (seirais) are ropes or chains; some manuscripts read sirois, pits. “Gloomy darkness” (zophos) is deep gloom, the darkness of the underworld. “Kept” (tēroumenous) is guarded, held in custody. Note that it is custody rather than sentence. They are held for a trial that has not yet happened, imprisoned now and awaiting final judgement (Jude 6; Revelation 20:10). Not all demons are bound, since many are active (Ephesians 6:12); these particular angels are.

Which angels are these? Some take them as the angels who fell with Satan at the beginning. Others, following Jewish tradition, link them with the sons of God who sinned with human women before the flood (Genesis 6:1–4), as Jude 6–7 may also do; and the order here (angels, then the flood, then Sodom) follows Genesis, which suggests the Genesis 6 sin. Calvin and many Reformed writers read the sons of God in Genesis 6 as the godly line of Seth instead. Peter does not stop to settle it, and we need not either. What is plain is that angels sinned, are now held for judgement, and will be judged. And the point stands either way: if God did not spare angels, he will not spare false teachers.

If he did not spare the ancient world. The second example: the flood (Genesis 6–8). Not one city now, but the whole world except one family.

But preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others. The second case adds the note that will govern the whole argument: God did not merely judge, he preserved. “Preserved” (ephylaxen) is guarded, protected, the first example of rescue. “Herald of righteousness” (dikaiosynēs kēryx) is a preacher of righteousness. Genesis records no sermon of Noah’s, but Jewish tradition held that he warned his generation, and Peter, by inspiration, confirms it (1 Peter 3:20). We may understand the building of the ark itself as a proclamation: years of hammering in the sight of neighbours who thought him mad, every plank a sermon about a coming flood. “With seven others” is literally the eighth: Noah and seven others, his wife, three sons and their wives. Peter counts the survivors, as in 1 Peter 3:20. He keeps returning to how few they were. Faithfulness is not measured by numbers.

When he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly. “Ungodly” (asebōn) means irreverent, without regard for God. The world of Noah’s day was not irreligious in the sense of having no gods; it simply lived as though the true God did not matter. Jesus said they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark (Matthew 24:38).

If by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction. The third example (Genesis 19), and the most public. “Turning to ashes” (tephrōsas) is reducing to ash. Their sins included sexual immorality and violence (Genesis 19:4–9; Jude 7), and also pride, excess and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49–50). So the three build: the highest creatures, the whole world, and the most notorious cities. If none of those was spared, the case Peter is making does not need arguing further.

Making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly. “Example” (hypodeigma) is a pattern set out for others to look at, a warning. The ruins by the Dead Sea functioned that way in Jewish memory for centuries. Past judgements are previews of the final judgement (Luke 17:26–30).

Is it not harsh to talk about judgement like this? It would be harsh only if it were untrue, or if it were said without tears. God’s judgement is not a flaw in his love but the expression of his holiness and justice; a God who never judged evil would not be good. And notice how Peter tells it: in every case judgement is accompanied by rescue, and it comes after long patience. God waited while Noah built; he would have spared Sodom for ten righteous people (Genesis 18:32). Speaking of judgement is a kindness when it moves people to flee to Christ, who bore it in their place. The cruel thing would be to stay silent.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is quick to judge. He waited patiently in Noah’s day (1 Peter 3:20) and would have spared Sodom for ten righteous people (Genesis 18:32). But his judgement does come.

In a sentence. For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but sent them to the deepest pit, putting them in chains of darkness to be held for judgement; if he did not spare the ancient world when he brought the flood on its ungodly people, but protected Noah, a preacher of righteousness, and seven others; if he condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah by burning them to ashes, and made them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;

On a Tuesday. Pray for those around you who are living as though there were no judgement: name three people. And if you feel foolish for believing in a coming day while everyone else carries on as normal, think of Noah’s hammer. He looked foolish for a long time. Then it rained.

For worship. The God who did not spare angels, nor the ancient world, nor the cities of the plain, is the God who did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all. Every judgement in this paragraph is a shadow of the one that fell on Calvary, and every rescue is a picture of what that judgement purchased. He shut Noah into the ark with his own hand. He will shut his people safely into Christ. Holy and just, patient and saving, he is the God who judges the world and preserves the few, and there is no ark but him.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” here is Tartarus, a Greek term for the deepest place of punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked (for as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard); then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment,
verseByVerse.commentary:
and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked (for as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard); then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment,

And if he rescued righteous Lot. This is the surprise of the paragraph, and it is worth pausing on, because Genesis does not present Lot flatteringly. He chose the well-watered plain and pitched his tent toward Sodom (Genesis 13:10–13); he offered his daughters to the mob (19:8); he lingered when the angels told him to flee, and had to be dragged out by the hand (19:16); and the story of his family afterwards is squalid (19:30–38). Yet Peter calls him righteous three times in two verses. That is a remarkable verdict, and it is not sentimentality. Lot was righteous by faith, as Abraham was, and God rescued him (Genesis 19:15–16, 29). It is the New Testament’s settled way of describing people who belong to God: not on the basis of their record but of their standing. If Lot is righteous, the word cannot mean impressive. “Rescued” (errysato) is delivered, drawn out, the word in the Lord’s Prayer: deliver us from evil.

Greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked. “Greatly distressed” (kataponoumenon) means worn down, oppressed, exhausted. “Sensual conduct” (aselgeia) is shameless immorality. “Wicked” (athesmōn) is lawless, unprincipled. Here is the evidence Peter goes on, and it is entirely inward. Lot did very little; what he did was suffer.

For as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard. Genesis does not tell of Lot’s inner distress, though Lot did protest the men’s demands (Genesis 19:7). Peter, by inspiration, reveals what Lot felt. “Tormenting” (ebasanizen) is a strong verb: torturing, vexing, the word for testing metal on a touchstone and for torment under interrogation. And day after day names the form it took: not one crisis but daily attrition, a man who had chosen to live there and could not stop being grieved by it. What he saw and heard got into him. Living in a wicked culture grieved him. Believers today should likewise be grieved, not entertained, by the wickedness around them.

A comfort for the compromised. This is a genuine encouragement to a believer who has made poor choices and is living in their consequences, and Peter surely intends it. If the mark of a righteous man in Sodom is that the place still distresses him, then the reader who feels worn down by the world around him has evidence rather than condemnation. The people who are comfortable are the ones in danger. And God rescued Lot even though he lingered: the angels seized him by the hand, the LORD being merciful to him (Genesis 19:16).

Then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials. Here is the conclusion of the long sentence (vv. 4–9), and both halves matter. “Knows how” (oiden): he has the wisdom and the power. The competence is his, and the readers do not have to work out the mechanism. “Rescue” (rhyesthai), as with Lot. “Godly” (eusebeis) is reverent, the word of 1:3, 6, 7. “Trials” (peirasmos) is testing, the same word as in 1 Peter 1:6. God will deliver his people, as he delivered Noah and Lot. He found a boat for one and a road out of the city for the other. He knows how.

And to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment. “Keep” (tērein) is hold in custody, the word of verse 4. The same providence does both: rescuing and keeping are one skill, not two. “Under punishment” (kolazomenous) is a present participle: being punished. The wicked who have died are already experiencing punishment, held for the final judgement (Luke 16:23–24). This supports a conscious intermediate state for the wicked as well as for the righteous: there is no soul sleep, and the dead are not unconscious until the last day. And it is real punishment, not purification: there is no purgatory here, only custody until the judgement.

What if I live, like Lot, somewhere I chose badly? First, take comfort: God did not abandon Lot, and he will not abandon you. Second, take warning: Lot lost much in Sodom: his possessions, his sons-in-law, his wife, and his daughters’ moral compass, and you can lose a great deal by staying where you are drawn into sin. Ask honestly whether your work, neighbourhood, friendships or entertainment are wearing down your love for God or merely wearing you down with grief. If the first, seek a way out, as God may be providing one. If the second, stay faithful, keep praying, and let your grief become prayer for the people around you.

How can I be grieved by the world without becoming bitter or self-righteous? Remember that Lot’s grief came from love of righteousness, not contempt for people. Grieve over sin as one who has been forgiven much, not as one who is better. Pray for those whose deeds trouble you, by name. Speak truth gently when you can. And turn your distress toward God, not toward endless complaining about the culture; Lot’s torment was in his soul before the Lord. A heart grieved by sin and full of mercy for sinners looks like Christ, who wept over Jerusalem.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will always be rescued from suffering in this life. It means God will finally rescue them, through death if necessary, and will never abandon them.

In a sentence. and if he rescued Lot, a righteous man, who was distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless (for that righteous man, living among them day after day, was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard), then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgement.

On a Tuesday. Notice what you saw and heard today: on the news, in the office, on a screen. Did any of it grieve you, or have you learned to enjoy what Lot found torment? Turn off one thing this week that you know entertains you with what God hates. And if you are weary from living among it, tell the Lord so, and remember that he knows how to rescue you.

For worship. He knows how. That is the whole comfort, and it is enough. The Lord who saw Lot lingering at the gate and took him by the hand is the Lord who sees his people today, worn down in their own Sodoms, and he has not forgotten one of them. He counts righteous those whose record is poor, because their righteousness is not their own but Christ’s. He hears the grief they never speak aloud. And he will bring every one of them out, by the hand if he must, before the fire falls.
verseByVerse.note: Genesis does not tell of Lot’s inner distress, though Lot did call the men’s intent wicked (Gen 19:7); Peter draws out the inner side of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–22 — The Portrait, and the Washed Sow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The false teachers scoff at spiritual powers that even angels treat with reverence. They act on instinct like animals, feast at the church’s meals while full of lust and greed, and follow Balaam, who loved money from wrongdoing. They are dry springs and rainless clouds, promising freedom while slaves of corruption. Having known the way of righteousness and turned back, they are worse off than before, like a dog returning to its vomit, or a washed pig to the mud.
verseByVerse.theology:
Washed, Not Changed

The false teachers promise freedom while slaves of corruption. The washed sow returns to the mire because her nature was never changed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Like Balaam, they loved gain and preyed on unsteady new believers.

Now: The question is not whether you have been washed, but whether you have been changed.

verseByVerse.quote: and especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority. Bold and willful, they do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones, whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority. Bold and willful, they do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones, whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord.

And especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion. Peter turns from the examples to the men themselves, and two marks come first. “Indulge” (poreuomenous) is literally go after, walk after: their desires lead and they follow. “Defiling passion” (epithymia miasmou) is desire of defilement, polluting lust: sexual immorality of various kinds, perhaps including perversions. The first mark is appetite.

And despise authority. “Authority” (kyriotēs) is lordship, dominion: either Christ’s lordship, or church authority, or angelic powers. They reject any authority over them. That is the second mark, and the one Peter develops. These men will not be told anything by anybody. And the two marks belong together: a man who wants to follow his appetites must first get rid of anyone who has the right to say no.

Bold and willful. “Bold” (tolmētai) is daring, audacious, reckless. “Willful” (authadeis) is self-willed, self-pleasing, arrogant, stubborn, as in Titus 1:7, where an elder must not be so. Together they describe a confidence that has no external check on it, which is exactly what makes a false teacher persuasive. Uncertain people are drawn to certainty, and these men never doubt themselves.

They do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones. “Glorious ones” (doxas, glories) are angelic beings, probably fallen angels or demons. The false teachers mock spiritual powers, speaking contemptuously of evil spirits, perhaps claiming that their freedom made them invulnerable. The point is not only what they said but the ease with which they said it. They speak about the unseen world casually, as men who have never considered that it might be real.

Whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord. Then the comparison, and it is devastating. Even holy angels, who actually know what these powers are, who are far stronger, and who outrank the men entirely, do not insult evil spirits but leave judgement to God. Jude 9 gives the example of the archangel Michael, who, disputing with the devil over Moses’ body, did not rebuke him himself but said, “The Lord rebuke you.” So the contrast is between beings who have seen the reality and are careful, and men who have seen nothing and are careless. Ignorance is producing the confidence. The false teachers are arrogant where angels are humble.

A lesson in reverence. There is a lesson here that outlives the original situation. A settled reverence about what one does not understand is a mark of spiritual maturity, and a readiness to talk loosely about the unseen is usually a sign of having thought about it very little. The same is true of the holy things of God: the man who jokes easily about judgement, hell or the devil has rarely looked at them long.

How should a Christian deal with the devil, then? Firmly, humbly, and in Christ’s name, not our own. Resist him, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:8–9; James 4:7). Put on the armour of God, which is truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation and the word (Ephesians 6:10–18). Pray. Flee temptation. You do not need to shout at demons, mock them, or seek them out; Michael simply appealed to the Lord. Nor do you need to fear them: greater is he who is in you (1 John 4:4). The posture is quiet confidence in Christ’s victory, not bravado and not terror.

What about authority I genuinely disagree with? Despising authority is not the same as disagreeing with it. You may question a decision, appeal respectfully, or, where an authority commands sin, obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Where authority is abused, especially in cases of abuse of the vulnerable, it must be exposed and the victims protected; that is not rebellion but righteousness. What Peter condemns is the settled heart that refuses to be under anyone, God included, so that it can do as it pleases.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should fear demons. Christ has triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15). It means believers should not be flippant or arrogant about spiritual powers, but resist them by faith in Christ’s authority, not their own.

In a sentence. This is especially true of those who follow the corrupt desire of the flesh and despise authority. Bold and arrogant, they are not afraid to heap abuse on celestial beings; yet even angels, although they are stronger and more powerful, do not heap abuse on such beings when bringing judgement on them from the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Is there any authority you despise: God’s, the church’s, legitimate human authority? Humble yourself before God this week. Notice also how you speak about holy things. If you joke about hell, mock the devil, or talk lightly of God’s judgement, ask the Lord for a reverent heart that trembles where trembling is right.

For worship. There is one before whom the mightiest angels cover their faces, and he is our Lord. Michael would not rebuke the devil in his own name, but appealed to him. At the name of Jesus every knee will bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth. He has disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them at the cross, so that his weakest child may resist the devil in his name and see him flee. All authority in heaven and earth is his, and it is in his authority, not our own, that we stand.

verseByVerse.quote: But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destruction, suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you. They have eyes full of adultery, insatiable for sin. They entice unsteady souls. They have hearts trained in greed. Accursed children!
verseByVerse.commentary:
But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destruction, suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you. They have eyes full of adultery, insatiable for sin. They entice unsteady souls. They have hearts trained in greed. Accursed children!

But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct. “Irrational” (aloga) is without reason, the very word logos negated. “Creatures of instinct” (gegennēmena physika) is literally born as natural creatures. The comparison is not merely abusive; it is diagnostic. An animal acts on appetite without deliberation, and Peter says that is precisely how these men operate. They claim superior knowledge but behave like animals driven only by appetite (Jude 10). They have exchanged reason for instinct, which is why arguing with them achieves nothing. And there is a sad irony set against chapter 1: believers were made partakers of the divine nature; these men have sunk to the merely natural.

Born to be caught and destroyed. Like wild animals that end in hunters’ traps. The animal follows its nose to the bait and never sees the snare. So do men who live by appetite.

Blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant. The charge of verse 10 restated, with the cause named: ignorance. They speak contemptuously of things they do not understand, and the less they understand, the louder they speak.

Will also be destroyed in their destruction. A wordplay: they will perish in their perishing, like animals. The ruin they bring on others is the ruin they receive.

Suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. Another wordplay: adikoumenoi misthon adikias, being wronged as the wage of wrong. They will receive exactly what they deserve. They wanted wages; they will get them. And the word for wage prepares for Balaam in verse 15.

They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. “Revel” (tryphē) is luxurious indulgence. A precise cultural detail. Even by the standards of a Greek city, serious drinking belonged to the night; daytime revelling was the mark of a man who had abandoned all restraint. Paul says the same: those who get drunk are drunk at night (1 Thessalonians 5:7). These people indulge shamelessly in broad daylight. Shame has gone.

They are blots and blemishes. “Blots” (spiloi) are stains, and “blemishes” (mōmoi) are disgraces, defects. This is a deliberate reversal. In his first letter Peter described Christ as a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:19), and in 3:14 he will urge believers to be found without spot or blemish. These men are the opposite, sitting at his table.

Reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you. There is the sting. “Deceptions” (apatais); some manuscripts read agapais, love feasts, as in Jude 12. The early church shared fellowship meals, often with the Lord’s Supper, and the false teachers took part, turning sacred fellowship into self-indulgence. This is happening at the church’s own meal, among the people of God, where the body and blood of Christ were remembered.

They have eyes full of adultery. The Greek is vivid: literally eyes full of an adulteress. A man who cannot look at a woman without assessing her; every woman they look at is a potential conquest (Matthew 5:28).

Insatiable for sin. “Insatiable” (akatapaustous) is unceasing, never resting. Sin never satisfies; it always wants more. That is the cruelty of every lust: it promises rest and delivers restlessness.

They entice unsteady souls. “Entice” (deleazontes) is the fishing and hunting word: to bait, to lure, as in James 1:14. And the target is named: “unsteady” (astēriktous), unstable, not established. It is the opposite of the established believers of 1:12. New or weak believers are their targets. Predators select carefully.

They have hearts trained in greed. “Trained” (gegymnasmenēn) is the athlete’s word, the root of gymnasium: exercised. Greed has been practised until it is skilled. This is not a lapse but a discipline, worked at until it comes naturally. The same word is used in Hebrews 5:14 of mature believers whose powers of discernment are trained by constant practice. Everyone is in training for something.

Accursed children! “Accursed children” (kataras tekna) is literally children of a curse: a Hebrew way of saying people under God’s curse. Peter’s exclamation is not a loss of temper but a cry of horror at what these men have become, and at where they are taking others.

Why is the Bible’s language about these men so harsh? Because the stakes are so high. These men are leading souls to destruction while feasting at the Lord’s Table. A doctor who discovers poison in the water supply does not describe it gently. Jesus spoke the same way of the scribes and Pharisees who shut the kingdom in people’s faces (Matthew 23). The harshness is love for the sheep. But note that it is aimed at those who teach and exploit, not at ordinary strugglers; to the weak and the wandering Scripture speaks with great tenderness (Matthew 12:20).

I struggle with lustful eyes. Am I like these men? There is a world of difference between a believer who fights lust and hates it, and a man whose eyes are full of it, who is insatiable, trains himself in it and teaches others to indulge. The first is a wounded soldier; the second is a deserter who has gone over to the enemy. If you are fighting, keep fighting: make a covenant with your eyes (Job 31:1), cut off what feeds it, bring it into the light with a trusted believer, and run to Christ each time you fall. The very fact that you grieve shows that you are not what this verse describes.

What it does not mean. The strong language does not license believers to insult opponents casually. Peter is giving an inspired, prophetic judgement on false teachers, to warn the church.

In a sentence. But these people blaspheme in matters they do not understand. They are like unreasoning animals, creatures of instinct, born only to be caught and destroyed, and like animals they too will perish. They will be paid back with harm for the harm they have done. Their idea of pleasure is to carouse in broad daylight. They are blots and blemishes, revelling in their pleasures while they feast with you. With eyes full of adultery, they never stop sinning; they seduce the unstable; they are experts in greed, an accursed brood!

On a Tuesday. Guard your eyes and your heart this week. Sin trained becomes sin mastered; godliness trained becomes godliness mastered. Ask what you are training yourself in by your habits: what you watch, what you scroll, what you spend on, what you daydream about. Replace one habit of the flesh with one habit of grace, and keep at it, because training takes repetition.

For worship. Against this portrait of blots and blemishes stands the Lamb without blemish or spot. His eyes were full of compassion, never lust; he was satisfied to do his Father’s will; he did not bait the unstable but gathered them, and carried the lambs in his arms. He was made a curse for us, so that children of a curse might become children of God. And his table, which these men defiled, he keeps for his people still, a feast of grace where the hungry are filled and the blemished are made clean.

verseByVerse.quote: Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor, who loved gain from wrongdoing, but was rebuked for his own transgression; a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet's madness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor, who loved gain from wrongdoing, but was rebuked for his own transgression; a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet’s madness.

Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. “Right way” (eutheia hodos) is the straight road. “Gone astray” (eplanēthēsan) is wandered, been deceived; the word gives us planet, a wandering star. They knew the road, and they left it.

They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor. Peter names the pattern, and Balaam is the exact case: a genuine prophet who put his gift on the market. The story is in Numbers 22–24. Balak of Moab offers money to have Israel cursed; Balaam keeps asking God for permission to go, and the narrative makes plain that he wants the fee. In the end he cannot curse; every time he opens his mouth, blessing comes out. But he later advises Balak how to lead Israel into sexual immorality and idolatry at Peor (Numbers 25:1–3; 31:16; Revelation 2:14), which is what he is remembered for. He became the classic example of a religious teacher who sells his gift for money and leads God’s people into sin (Jude 11).

Who loved gain from wrongdoing. “Loved gain from wrongdoing” (misthon adikias ēgapēsen) is literally loved the wages of unrighteousness, echoing verse 13. That is Peter’s summary, and it identifies the false teachers precisely: not men who set out to destroy the church but men who discovered that religion pays and adjusted their message to keep it paying. Money was Balaam’s god. And notice the verb: loved. The problem was not that he was paid, but what he loved.

But was rebuked for his own transgression. “Rebuked” (elenxin eschen) is received conviction, rebuke. “Transgression” (paranomia) is lawbreaking, going against what he knew.

A speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet’s madness. Peter tells it with a certain relish. “Speechless” (aphōnon) is voiceless: a voiceless beast of burden producing a human voice, and the reversal is the point. The irrational animal of verse 12 had more sense than the prophet. The prophet is behaving like an animal, so an animal has to do the prophet’s job (Numbers 22:21–35). And the false teachers are like Balaam, with less sense than a donkey. “Madness” (paraphronia) is insanity, being out of one’s mind. A hard word, and Peter chooses it deliberately. Balaam was not deceived; he had heard from God repeatedly and went anyway. That is not error, it is derangement, and the man who knows exactly what God has said and calculates that the money is worth it has lost his reason, whatever his gifts.

The mercy in the road. There is a mercy in the story too, easily missed. The donkey and the angel were sent to stop him. The angel stood in the road with a drawn sword, and the donkey turned aside three times and saved his life (Numbers 22:33). Even a man this far gone was given an obstacle in the road. God often puts such obstacles in our way: a closed door, a rebuke, an illness, a word from an unexpected mouth. The question is whether we beat the donkey or listen to it.

How do I know whether I love money too much? Ask a few honest questions. Would I compromise truth or conscience to keep or gain it? Do I give generously and gladly, or grudgingly? Does the thought of losing it fill me with fear? Does it shape my decisions more than God’s word does? Do I resent others who have more? Love of money is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:10), and it hides well, especially in religious people. The cure is not only to hold it loosely but to love something better: to find Christ so satisfying that money returns to its proper place as a tool and not a god.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all who are paid for ministry are like Balaam. Workers deserve wages (1 Timothy 5:18). The sin is loving money and compromising truth for it.

In a sentence. They have left the straight way and wandered off to follow the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness. But he was rebuked for his wrongdoing by a donkey, an animal without speech, who spoke with a human voice and restrained the prophet’s madness.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last time someone corrected you, especially someone you thought beneath you: a child, a junior colleague, a stranger. Did you beat the donkey or listen to it? Go back and thank them if they were right. And look at your bank statement this week as a spiritual document: what does it say you love?

For worship. Balaam was hired to curse, and God would not let him: every curse turned to blessing in his mouth, because the Lord your God loved Israel. That is the God we serve. No hireling, no false prophet, no enemy can curse those whom he has blessed. And he is merciful even to the mad, placing angels and donkeys in the road. One came who was offered all the kingdoms of the world and refused them, who had nowhere to lay his head and made many rich. He did not love the wages of unrighteousness. He paid the wages of ours.
verseByVerse.note: Balaam was hired to curse Israel for money, and his donkey spoke to rebuke him.

verseByVerse.quote: These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved. For, speaking loud boasts of folly, they entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error. They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption. For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved. For, speaking loud boasts of folly, they entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error. They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption. For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.

These are waterless springs. Two images, and both are about promise without delivery. “Springs” (pēgai) are fountains. In that country a spring was life. To walk to one in the heat and find it dry is not disappointment but danger. Peter is describing men whose teaching offers exactly what a thirsty person needs and has nothing in it. God had complained through Jeremiah that his people had forsaken him, the fountain of living waters, and dug broken cisterns that can hold no water (Jeremiah 2:13). False teachers are such cisterns.

And mists driven by a storm. The second is the same failure in the sky. “Mists” (homichlai) are haze, fog. Clouds driven by a squall raise every farmer’s hope and pass over without rain, and Jude uses the same picture (Jude 12). They look like rain clouds but are blown away without giving rain. These men are weather that does not break: all promise, no substance.

For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved. “Gloom of utter darkness” (ho zophos tou skotous) is the blackness of darkness. The destiny of the false teachers is eternal darkness, outer darkness (Matthew 8:12; 22:13; Jude 13). “Reserved” (tetērētai) is the custody word from verses 4 and 9, kept, perfect tense: set aside and waiting. And there is a grim fitness: men who promised light are held in the dark.

For, speaking loud boasts of folly. “Loud boasts” (hyperonka) are swelling, inflated, bombastic words. “Folly” (mataiotēs) is emptiness, futility, the word Paul uses of creation subjected to futility (Romans 8:20). Impressive-sounding but empty, like a drum. The promise is delivered confidently, which is what makes it work on people who are unsure.

They entice by sensual passions of the flesh. “Entice” (deleazousin) is bait, as in verse 14. The bait is not intellectual; it is appetite: sensual pleasure. The method is stated exactly.

Those who are barely escaping from those who live in error. “Barely escaping” (oligōs apopheugontas) is just escaping, only a little escaping: new converts who have just left paganism. They are most vulnerable. That is the cruelty of it. New converts, still unsteady, having just broken with a way of life at real cost, are told they need not have bothered.

They promise them freedom. “Freedom” (eleutheria) is probably a twisted version of Christian freedom, claiming that grace means freedom from moral rules (Galatians 5:13; 1 Peter 2:16; Romans 6:1–2). It is the oldest lie in the world, the serpent’s promise in the garden: throw off God’s word and your eyes will be opened.

But they themselves are slaves of corruption. “Slaves” (douloi). “Corruption” (phthora) is moral decay, as in 1:4, where believers escaped the corruption that is in the world. Those who promise freedom are themselves enslaved. The irony is the sharpest thing in the chapter: Peter called himself a slave of Christ in 1:1, and these men, who mock such slavery, are slaves of rot.

For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved. “Overcomes” (hēttētai) is defeats, masters, a word from the battlefield: the conquered become the slaves of the conqueror. A proverb, and one of the truest sentences in the letter: whatever masters you is your master (John 8:34; Romans 6:16). Freedom is not the absence of a master; it is a question of which one. The man who has thrown off restraint has not become free. He has changed owners, and taken a worse one. Sin is not freedom; it is slavery.

What does real Christian freedom look like? It is freedom from the guilt of sin, because Christ has paid for it; freedom from the power of sin, because we are united to him; freedom from the law as a way of earning acceptance; and freedom from fear of death and judgement. But it is freedom for something: to love God and serve others (Galatians 5:13). A train is free on its rails and helpless off them; a fish is free in water and dies on the bank. We are free when we live as we were made to live, under the gentle rule of Christ, whose yoke is easy.

I have just come to faith and feel shaky. How do I avoid being lured? Stay close to the flock and to faithful shepherds; predators pick off the sheep that wander alone. Get into a Bible-teaching church and attend faithfully. Read Scripture daily, starting with a Gospel. Find an older believer to meet with and ask questions. Be wary of anyone who tells you that the sins you have left were not really so bad, or that grace means you need not change. And when temptation comes dressed as freedom, ask where it leads; the end of the road is what tells you the truth about it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christian freedom is false. Christ truly sets us free (John 8:36; Galatians 5:1). But freedom is from sin, not freedom to sin.

In a sentence. These people are springs without water and mists driven by a storm. Blackest darkness is reserved for them. For they mouth empty, boastful words and, by appealing to the lustful desires of the flesh, they entice people who are just escaping from those who live in error. They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves of depravity, for people are slaves to whatever has mastered them.

On a Tuesday. What masters you? If anything other than Christ controls you, bring it to him for freedom. Name the thing you reach for without thinking when you are bored, anxious or lonely; that is often the master. Then tell Christ plainly that you want him to rule there, and take one practical step to break its grip.

For worship. Christ is not a dry spring. He stood up on the last day of the feast and cried out, if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink, and from him rivers of living water flow. He is not a mist that passes over; he comes down like rain on the mown grass. He does not promise freedom and enslave; he became a slave to set slaves free, and the Son who sets us free makes us free indeed. Every other master devours; this one gives his life for those he rules, and his service is perfect freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first. For it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. What the true proverb says has happened to them: "The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first. For it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. What the true proverb says has happened to them: “The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire.”

For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world. These verses are among the most sobering in the New Testament, and they must be allowed their weight before anything is done to soften them. “They” are the false teachers, and perhaps those they led astray. “Escaped” (apophygontes) is the word of 1:4. “Defilements” (miasmata) are pollutions. They had outwardly left their former life of sin. The language of escape is real: whatever these men were, they were not outsiders. They had genuinely got out, at the level anyone could see.

Through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. “Knowledge” (epignōsis), the letter’s key word. They had known the gospel, understood it, perhaps professed it. They had genuinely known, in the sense of acquaintance with the truth.

They are again entangled in them and overcome. “Entangled” (emplakentes) is woven in, caught, like a fish in a net or a man in thorns. “Overcome” (hēttōntai) is defeated, as in verse 19. They have been conquered again by the master they once escaped.

The last state has become worse for them than the first. Peter is quoting his Master. The Lord said the same about a house swept clean and reoccupied by seven worse spirits, so that the last state is worse than the first (Matthew 12:45; Luke 11:26). Having known the truth and rejected it, they are more guilty and more hardened than before.

For it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness. That is the plain sense, and it should not be blunted. Greater knowledge brings greater responsibility (Luke 12:47–48; Hebrews 6:4–6; 10:26–29). Knowledge raises the stakes; a man who has seen and turned away is in a worse position than one who never saw.

Than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. “Turn back” (hypostrepsai) is return. “Holy commandment” is the Christian faith and way of life, delivered by the apostles (Jude 3). It was handed to them, like a precious thing passed from hand to hand, and they put it down.

What the true proverb says has happened to them. “True proverb” (alēthēs paroimia). How does this stand with the perseverance of the saints? Peter himself supplies the answer, and it is the reason the proverb is there.

The dog returns to its own vomit. From Proverbs 26:11. Dogs in the ancient world were not pets but scavengers, despised as unclean. The dog gets rid of what was making it sick, and then goes back to it, because it is still a dog.

And the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire. A popular proverb. Look at what has and has not changed. The sow has been washed: genuinely, outwardly, and everyone could see it. What she has not been given is a different nature. She returns to the mud because she is still a pig, and washing a pig does not make it a sheep. These two proverbs explain the passage: the false teachers were outwardly cleaned, but their nature was never changed. They were dogs and pigs all along, never sheep. That is Peter’s verdict on such men: not that they lost salvation, but that they were cleaned rather than changed. The escape was real at the level of behaviour, and the heart was never renewed, which is exactly what 1 John 2:19 says of those who went out from us because they were not of us.

Where Christians differ: does this passage show that true believers can lose salvation? Arminian Christians read the passage so, pointing to escaped and to knowledge of our Lord and Saviour. Verdict: The proverbs answer the question. The dog and the sow returned to filth because their nature had never been changed; they were washed outwardly but remained dogs and pigs. These people had external knowledge of Christ and outward moral reform, but never received a new nature (1:4). True believers, made partakers of the divine nature, are kept by God’s power (1 Peter 1:5) and will never finally fall (1:10). Those who return permanently to their former life show they were never truly regenerated (1 John 2:19).

How can someone know so much and never be truly saved? Because knowing about Christ is not the same as being united to him. Judas walked with Jesus for three years, heard every sermon and saw every miracle. People can be moved by the gospel, reform their habits, join a church, even teach, and yet never have been born again (Matthew 7:21–23; 13:20–21). The difference is not how much they knew but whether the Spirit gave them a new heart. That is why the test is not how impressive a conversion looked, but what a person keeps returning to over time.

I have gone back to an old sin. Am I the dog returning to its vomit? Not if you hate it and want to be free. The dog returns to its vomit gladly, because it is what a dog loves. A child of God may fall back into sin, sometimes badly and repeatedly, but he is miserable there, he confesses it, and he longs to be clean (Psalm 51; 1 John 1:9). Peter himself denied Christ three times and was restored. If you are grieved, go to Christ today. He has not changed his mind about you, and the new nature in you is the very thing that makes the mud unbearable.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer who sins after conversion is lost. All believers stumble (James 3:2). The issue is a settled, final return to a life of sin, rejecting the truth.

In a sentence. If they have escaped the corruption of the world by knowing our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ and are again entangled in it and overcome, they are worse off at the end than they were at the beginning. It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than to have known it and then to turn their backs on the sacred command passed on to them. Of them the proverbs are true: “A dog returns to its vomit,” and, “A sow that is washed returns to her wallowing in the mud.”

On a Tuesday. The pastoral use of this passage is not to make secure believers anxious but to make everyone honest. The question it puts is not whether you have been washed. It is whether you have been changed, and the evidence is what you find yourself returning to. When you are tired, alone and unwatched, where do your thoughts and feet go? Thank God for every sign that you now love what you once hated; and where the old pull remains, bring it to him today.

For worship. He did not merely wash us; he made us new. A washed pig is still a pig, but the Lord Jesus does not wash pigs and leave them pigs. He gives a new heart and puts a new spirit within, and makes sinners partakers of his own holy life, so that what they once loved becomes their grief, and what they once despised becomes their joy. He who began that work will finish it. The dog returns to its vomit; the sheep returns to its Shepherd, because his voice is the one it now loves, and no one will snatch it out of his hand.

2.theology: The chapter's controlling theological question is the nature of apostasy. Can a person who has genuinely known Christ fall finally away? The Reformed answer: those truly regenerate will persevere (John 10:28–29; Rom 8:38–39). But the visible church contains those who participate in covenant privileges without possessing covenant life — and it is these who can experience the knowledge described in v. 20 and still return to their former state. The dog and pig proverbs define the boundary: the animal's nature is unchanged. External reformation without regeneration leads to greater corruption. This is not a loophole in the doctrine of perseverance; it is the doctrine's honest context.
2.examples: The Balaam portrait (vv. 15–16) gives the congregation diagnostic tools. The false teacher's test is not doctrinal sophistication but financial transparency: What does this teacher gain from what he teaches? Is the teaching shaped by what people want to hear (and therefore what they will pay to hear)? Balaam was a genuine prophet whose gift was real — but the gift became a commodity. The test of authentic ministry is not whether the gifts are real but whether the teacher loves the Lord more than the wages.

3.title: The Day That Is Coming
3.overview:
The last chapter is the letter’s goal. The false teachers are dangerous because they attack the hope of Christ’s return, and with it the reason for holy living. If no day is coming, why be holy?

Peter answers in three steps. The world has not always continued as it was: God’s word created it and judged it by the flood, and the same word holds it now for judgment. God is not slow, but patient, giving time for repentance. And the day will come suddenly and lay everything bare. So the question is not “When?” but “What sort of people ought you to be?” The letter ends: grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever.
3.text: <sup>1</sup>This is now the second letter that I am writing to you, beloved. In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder,<sup>2</sup>that you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles,<sup>3</sup>knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires.<sup>4</sup>They will say, "Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation."<sup>5</sup>For they deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God,<sup>6</sup>and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished.<sup>7</sup>But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire, being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly.<sup>8</sup>But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.<sup>9</sup>The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.<sup>10</sup>But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.<sup>11</sup>Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness,<sup>12</sup>waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn!<sup>13</sup>But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.<sup>14</sup>Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace.<sup>15</sup>And count the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him,<sup>16</sup>as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures.<sup>17</sup>You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, take care that you are not carried away with the error of lawless people and lose your own stability.<sup>18</sup>But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Scoffers and the Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter writes to remind them of the prophets and the apostles’ teaching. Scoffers will come, following their desires, saying, “Where is the promise of his coming?” They choose to forget that God’s word created the world and destroyed it by the flood, and that the same word now holds the heavens and earth for the fire of judgment. With the Lord a day is as a thousand years. He is not slow but patient, wanting all to come to repentance. And the day will come like a thief.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not Slowness but Patience

The world has not always continued as it was: God's word made it and judged it by the flood. The Lord is not slow but patient, and the day will come like a thief.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Scoffers pointed to the death of the first generation as proof that nothing was coming.

Now: The delay is mercy; the right response is repentance, not argument about the timetable.

verseByVerse.quote: This is now the second letter that I am writing to you, beloved. In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder, that you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles,
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is now the second letter that I am writing to you, beloved. In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder, that you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles,

Meaning first. 2 Peter 3 answers the false teachers’ denial of Christ’s return and calls believers to holy living as they wait. Peter writes to remind them of the prophets’ predictions and the apostles’ teaching (vv. 1–2). Scoffers will come, living for their desires and mocking the promise of his coming and claiming that nothing has changed since creation (vv. 3–4). But they deliberately ignore that God created the world by his word and judged it once by water; by the same word the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire on the day of judgement (vv. 5–7). God does not measure time as we do: a day is like a thousand years to him; his apparent delay is patience, not wanting any to perish but all to come to repentance (vv. 8–9). The day of the Lord will come like a thief; the heavens will pass away, the elements will melt, and the earth and its works will be exposed (v. 10). Since everything will be dissolved, believers should live holy and godly lives, looking forward to and hastening that day, and to new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells (vv. 11–13). So they should be diligent to be found spotless and at peace, regarding the Lord’s patience as salvation, as Paul also wrote, whose letters the unstable twist as they do the other Scriptures (vv. 14–16). The letter ends with a final warning not to be carried away by error, and a final command: grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be glory now and forever (vv. 17–18). It is the last chapter an old apostle wrote, and it looks past his own death, past the scoffers, past the fire, to a world where righteousness is at home.

This is now the second letter that I am writing to you, beloved. The earlier letter is most likely 1 Peter. Peter treats both letters as one project with one aim. “Beloved” (agapētoi) is used four times in this chapter (vv. 1, 8, 14, 17), a warm contrast with the harsh words about false teachers. Having described the wolves, the shepherd turns to the sheep and his voice changes. Every warning in this chapter is spoken to people he loves.

In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder. “Stirring up” (diegeirō) is rousing, waking, the waking verb again from 1:13. Peter’s settled view of his ministry is that his readers do not need new material; they need rousing. “Sincere” (eilikrinē) is a striking word here: pure, unmixed, often explained as judged by sunlight, as pottery was held up to the sun to check for cracks, or cloth to find flaws in the weave. It is what a thing looks like when the light gets behind it. “Mind” (dianoia) is understanding. Unlike the false teachers, the readers have pure minds, and Peter credits them with genuineness even as he warns them. But they still need reminding. A sound mind is not a mind beyond the reach of drowsiness.

That you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets. “Predictions” (proeirēmenōn rhēmatōn) are words spoken beforehand. The Old Testament prophets foretold the Day of the Lord, judgement and new creation (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; Joel 2; Daniel 7; 12). And the whole defence against what follows is memory: not a new argument but the recollection of what they were already told.

And the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles. “Commandment” (entolē) is the apostolic teaching, including Christ’s promise to return. “Through your apostles”: the apostles are Christ’s mouthpieces. Note your apostles: not a distant institution but the men who actually brought them the gospel. And here are two authorities, set side by side without any suggestion that they differ in weight: the Old Testament prophets, and the apostles carrying the Lord’s own commandment. Peter places the apostles’ teaching alongside the Old Testament prophets as equally authoritative. That is a significant sentence for how the early church understood its own writings, and Peter will do it explicitly with Paul’s letters in verse 16. The two together, Old Testament and New, form the foundation (Ephesians 2:20).

Why does it matter that the prophets and apostles are put together? Because it means the whole Bible speaks with one voice and one authority. The Old Testament is not a lesser, outdated book, and the New Testament is not merely the church’s opinion about Jesus. Both are God’s word. So when you read about the day of the Lord in Joel or Zephaniah and then in Peter, you are hearing one story told by one Author, promised in the one and explained in the other. Read them together, and let each shed light on the other.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the apostles invented new commandments. They delivered what Christ commanded (Matthew 28:20).

In a sentence. Dear friends, this is now my second letter to you. I have written both of them as reminders to stimulate you to wholesome thinking. I want you to recall the words spoken in the past by the holy prophets and the command given by our Lord and Saviour through your apostles.

On a Tuesday. Pick one promise of Christ’s return, from the prophets or the apostles, and read it each morning this week: Acts 1:11, John 14:3, or Isaiah 65:17–25. Let it wake you. And thank God for whoever first brought you the apostles’ message; that person was your Peter.

For worship. God did not leave his people with a single voice crying in the dark. He spoke through the holy prophets century after century, and then through his Son, and through the apostles his Son sent, and all of it was one word, pointing to one day and one Lord. He loves his people too much to let them forget. He keeps waking us, by letters written long ago, so that minds held up to his light may be found pure on the day he comes.
