verseByVerse.quote: knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires. They will say, "Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires. They will say, “Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation.”

Knowing this first of all. As in 1:20. Of first importance, before you hear the scoffers, know that they were foretold.

That scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing. “Scoffers” (empaiktai) are mockers, ridiculers. “With scoffing” (en empaigmonē) is in mockery: mockers mocking, a Hebrew-style emphasis. And Peter says their arrival is itself predicted. That is a quietly clever move: the appearance of people denying the promise is evidence that the promise was accurately given. Every scoffer is, without meaning to be, a fulfilled prophecy. “Last days”: the whole period since Christ’s first coming (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2; Jude 18). The scoffers were already present in Peter’s day, and they are with us still.

Following their own sinful desires. Peter names the motive before he states the argument, and the order is deliberate. Their doctrine has a cause, and the cause is not intellectual. Here is the link between denying judgement and indulging desires: if there is no coming judgement, there is no reason to restrain oneself. Their theology serves their lusts. A man who wants the future to be empty has a reason for wanting it.

They will say, Where is the promise of his coming? Then the taunt itself. “Promise of his coming” (hē epangelia tēs parousias autou) is Jesus’ promise to return (John 14:3; Acts 1:11). The mocking question echoes Old Testament scoffers, who asked the psalmist all the day long where his God was (Psalm 42:3), and who asked, where is the God of justice? (Malachi 2:17).

For ever since the fathers fell asleep. “The fathers” are probably the first generation of Christians, who had died, or perhaps the Old Testament patriarchs. “Fell asleep” (ekoimēthēsan) means died, a common Christian euphemism (1 Thessalonians 4:13–15) that already carries the hope of waking. The argument has two parts and both would have stung. The first is that the first generation had died and nothing had happened. Decades had passed; Christ had not come. It was a real pastoral problem in a church burying its founders.

All things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation. “Continuing” (diamenei) is remaining unchanged. And the second part is a philosophy: things go on as they always have. It is the argument from uniformity: the world is a closed system running on unbroken regularity; God does not intervene; what has never been observed to happen therefore does not happen; there will be no judgement. That is a very modern-sounding argument to find in a first-century letter, and a view still common today. Peter’s answer, when it comes, does not dispute the observation that the sun rises every morning. He disputes the conclusion, and he does it by pointing to two occasions when things did not continue as they were.

Is it wrong to wonder why Christ has not yet come? No. Honest questions are not scoffing. The souls under the altar cry, how long? (Revelation 6:10), and the psalms are full of it. What Peter condemns is mocking unbelief that uses the delay as an excuse to live as one pleases. The difference lies in the heart: the scoffer asks where is he? hoping the answer is nowhere; the believer asks where is he? because he longs to see him. If your question comes from longing, it is a kind of prayer: come, Lord Jesus.

How should I answer someone who says the world just runs by natural laws? Agree that the world is wonderfully regular, and then ask why. The regularity of nature is not an argument against God but evidence of his faithful upholding of all things by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3; Genesis 8:22). Laws describe how things normally go; they do not forbid the Lawgiver from acting. And history itself is not a closed loop: it had a beginning, it has seen a resurrection, and Scripture says it is moving toward an end. Be gentle, and point the conversation to Jesus’ resurrection, which is the decisive interruption.

What it does not mean. It does not mean honest questions about the timing of Christ’s return are scoffing. Scoffing is mocking unbelief that rejects God’s promise in order to justify sin.

In a sentence. Above all, you must understand that in the last days scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires. They will say, “Where is this ‘coming’ he promised? Ever since our ancestors died, everything goes on as it has since the beginning of creation.”

On a Tuesday. Have you ever been mocked for believing Christ will return? Don’t be shaken; Scripture said it would happen. And check your own heart: is there any area of your life where you live as though he were not coming, because you would rather he did not see it yet? Bring that into the light today.

For worship. The scoffers say nothing changes. But the Lord who made all things from nothing, who raised his Son from the tomb, and who has promised to come again is not bound by the regularity he himself sustains. Every sunrise is his faithfulness, and every sunrise brings his coming one day nearer. The fathers fell asleep, and they will wake. The promise has not lapsed, because the One who made it cannot lie, and the mockers themselves stand as witnesses that his word was true.

verseByVerse.quote: For they deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God, and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished. But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire, being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God, and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished. But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire, being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly.

For they deliberately overlook this fact. “Deliberately overlook” (lanthanei thelontas) means this escapes their notice because they want it to: they wilfully forget. Their ignorance is chosen (Romans 1:18–21). Peter does not accuse them of missing the evidence but of declining to look at it, which is the more serious charge.

That the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God. What they overlook is creation itself. The first fact they ignore: God made the world by his word (Genesis 1; Hebrews 11:3). “Out of water and through water”: in Genesis 1 the earth emerged from the waters (1:2, 6–10). The world is not self-existent or eternal; it depends on God’s word. The claim that all things continue as they were from the beginning of creation collapses at the word creation. There was a beginning, and it was not a continuation of anything.

And that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished. The second fact they ignore: the flood. “By means of these” (di’ hōn): by water and the word. “Deluged” (kataklystheis) is flooded, from which comes cataclysm. “Perished” (apōleto) is was destroyed. The same water that the world was formed through later destroyed it, which is exactly a case of things not continuing as they were. The world did not continue unchanged; God judged it once. So the argument is complete in two strokes. The scoffers say nothing has ever interrupted the regularity; Peter names two occasions when the world’s entire state was changed by the word of God, and both are in the Scriptures the scoffers claim to respect.

Was the flood worldwide? Some Christians hold that it covered the whole inhabited region rather than the whole earth. But Genesis says all the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered (Genesis 7:19), and Peter sets the flood beside the coming judgement of the whole earth by fire. The more likely reading is that the flood was universal.

But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire. The phrase the same word is the hinge of the whole passage. One agency made it, one flooded it, and one holds it now. God’s word that created and judged will judge again. The present stability is not inertia; it is sustained, and by the same voice that could end it. “Stored up” (tethēsaurismenoi) is reserved, treasured up, as in a treasury. “For fire”: the next judgement will be by fire, not water. God promised Noah never again to destroy the earth by a flood (Genesis 9:11), and the prophets speak of fire (Isaiah 66:15–16; Malachi 4:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–8).

Being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly. “Kept” (tēroumenoi) is guarded, preserved, the custody word again, as of the angels in 2:4. Peter’s picture of the present universe is not a machine running down but something held in reserve. God is holding the present world until judgement. “Destruction” (apōleia) is perdition, ruin. For the ungodly, eternal ruin.

What it does not mean. Destruction does not mean annihilation of the ungodly. Scripture describes their punishment as eternal and conscious (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11; 20:10). The word means ruin, loss of all that makes existence good.

Should a Christian fear that the world will end in a nuclear war or climate disaster? We should care for God’s creation and work for peace, because we are stewards of what he made. But we need not live in terror that human beings will end the world before God’s time. The heavens and earth are kept by his word for his day. History will not end by accident or by our hand, but when and as he has appointed. That frees us both from despair and from the burden of thinking we must save the planet ourselves. Do your duty calmly, and trust the Keeper.

In a sentence. But they deliberately forget that long ago by God’s word the heavens came into being and the earth was formed out of water and by water. By these waters also the world of that time was deluged and destroyed. By the same word the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire, being kept for the day of judgement and destruction of the ungodly.

On a Tuesday. When you hear the world spoken of as though it runs itself, remember the same word. Thank God at the start of the day that he is holding all things together, and at the end of the day that he has kept them one more day for the sake of mercy. And ask whether there is anything you are deliberately overlooking because you would rather not see it.

For worship. He spoke, and the waters parted and the dry land appeared. He spoke again, and the fountains of the deep broke open. He speaks still, and the stars keep their courses and the earth its seasons, held in reserve by the word that made them. The same word became flesh, and bore in his own body the judgement of fire for all who trust him. What is stored up for the ungodly is wrath; what is stored up for his people is an inheritance kept in heaven. Blessed be the Word of God, by whom all things were made and in whom all things hold together.

verseByVerse.quote: But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.

But do not overlook this one fact, beloved. “Do not overlook” (mē lanthanetō) is do not let it escape you, the same verb he used of the scoffers in verse 5, now turned round with an endearment attached. The scoffers deliberately forget; believers must not. They overlook; do not you overlook this.

That with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The line echoes Psalm 90:4: a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday when it is past. God is not bound by time as we are. He is eternal. What seems a long delay to us is nothing to him. Equally, he can accomplish in a day what would take us a thousand years. The point: we must not judge God’s faithfulness by our timetable. To a creature with seventy or eighty years, a delay of two millennia seems decisive; to the One who made time it is not a delay at all. The scoffers’ argument depends entirely on assuming God experiences duration the way they do.

Both halves are needed. The comparison runs both ways, which would make any arithmetic useless. A thousand years as one day means the long wait is nothing to him. One day as a thousand years means no single day is trivial to him either: he is not distracted or inattentive during the interval. He gives each day of your life the attention of a thousand years.

Where Christians differ: does this verse teach a thousand-year day or a millennial scheme? Some have used this verse to calculate the timing of Christ’s return, such as six thousand years of history followed by a thousand-year millennium. Verdict: The verse is not a formula for calculation; it teaches that God’s perspective on time differs from ours. It warns against date-setting, not encourages it (Matthew 24:36; Acts 1:7). It gives no support to elaborate millennial timetables.

Does this mean that the days of creation were long ages? This verse does not say so. Peter is speaking of how God relates to time, to explain the delay of Christ’s coming; the verse is not a conversion table, and reading it as one has produced a great deal of confusion. The days of Genesis 1 must be read from Genesis itself; many read them as ordinary days (Exodus 20:11), and Reformed Christians differ somewhat on their length, while agreeing that God made all things by his word. Whatever view a Christian takes of that question, this verse does not settle it, because it is not about creation at all.

Why would God make his people wait so long? Peter gives the main answer in the next verse: patience, so that more may repent. But consider too that waiting is how God grows faith. Abraham waited twenty-five years for Isaac; Israel waited centuries for the Messiah; Simeon waited all his life to hold the child. In the waiting, God tests and refines his people, teaches them to walk by faith and not sight, and gathers in his elect. The wait is long to us, but it is not empty. It is full of his purposes.

What it does not mean. It does not mean time is meaningless to God, or that day in Scripture always means a thousand years. It means God sees time from eternity, and his promises are not delayed by our standards.

In a sentence. But do not forget this one thing, dear friends: with the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day.

On a Tuesday. When God seems slow, remember: he sees all time at once. Trust his perfect timing. Think of a prayer you have prayed for years without an answer. Pray it again today, not with resignation but with confidence that he has not forgotten one day of it. And treat today as he does: not as a small, forgettable day, but as one in which a thousand years’ worth of faithfulness can be shown.

For worship. Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever he had formed the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting he is God. Our years are a breath to him, and yet he numbers our hairs and counts our tears. He is above time, and he entered time, and for thirty-three years the Eternal was measured in days. He is not late. He has never been late. When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son; and when the fullness of time comes again, he will send him once more.

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.

The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness. “Slow” (bradynei) is delay, loiter. Peter denies the premise directly, and note the qualifier: as some count. The slowness exists only in the reckoning of the people complaining. The scoffers interpret delay as failure. But the delay has a purpose.

But is patient toward you. Here is the positive answer, the great sentence of the chapter. “Patient” (makrothymei) is long-suffering, slow to anger, literally long of temper. “Toward you” (eis hymas): the readers, God’s beloved people (v. 1), the chosen (1 Peter 1:1). God delays for their sake. The delay is not indifference, not incapacity, and not forgetfulness. It is patience, and it is directed at them. That reframes the whole complaint. Every day the end has not come is a day granted. The scoffers were treating the interval as evidence against God; Peter says it is evidence of his mercy, and that they are standing inside the very thing they are mocking.

Not wishing that any should perish. “Wishing” (boulomenos) is willing, desiring. “Perish” (apolesthai) is be destroyed. God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 18:23, 32; 33:11).

But that all should reach repentance. “Reach” (chōrēsai) is come to, make room for. “Repentance” (metanoia) is change of mind and direction. God’s patience gives time for repentance (Romans 2:4).

Where Christians differ: if God wishes all to repent, why are not all saved? Arminians read this verse as showing that God wills every individual to be saved and that human choice makes the difference; universalists as showing that all will eventually be saved. Verdict: The context helps: God is patient toward you, addressing believers, the beloved, the elect. The delay of Christ’s return is so that all of God’s people, including those not yet converted, may come to repentance before the end. When the last of the elect has been brought in, Christ will return. At the same time, Scripture teaches that God sincerely desires the repentance of all sinners in the sense that he delights in repentance and offers the gospel freely to all (Ezekiel 33:11; 1 Timothy 2:4), while he has also sovereignly chosen to save some and not all. These two truths, God’s revealed desire and his decreed purpose, are both taught, and must both be held. Universalism contradicts the next verse and the clear teaching of eternal judgement.

The use of the verse. On either emphasis the pastoral use is the same, which is presumably why Peter wrote it. What neither permits is the conclusion the scoffers wanted, that the delay means nothing is coming. If God is holding the door open, the response of anyone still outside it is not to argue about the mechanism but to walk through.

If God has chosen his elect, why should I evangelise? Because God has chosen the means as well as the end. The elect are brought to repentance through the gospel being preached (Romans 10:14–17), and God waits so that the gospel may reach them. Election is the great encouragement to evangelism, not its enemy: Paul was told to keep speaking in Corinth because the Lord had many people in that city (Acts 18:9–10). You do not know who the elect are, so offer Christ freely to everyone, sincerely, as God himself does. Every day of patience is a day for the gospel.

I have a loved one who has not repented. Is it too late? Not while they are alive, and not while the Lord is patient. This verse is a reason to keep praying and keep loving. God waited for you, perhaps for years. He knows how to bring the hardest heart to repentance, as he did with Saul of Tarsus. So pray specifically, live kindly before them, speak of Christ when doors open, and leave the timing with God. His patience is not reluctance to save; it is room being made for repentance.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is unable to accomplish what he wants. It means his patience serves his purpose of bringing his people to repentance.

In a sentence. The Lord is not slow in keeping his promise, as some understand slowness. Instead he is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish, but everyone to come to repentance.

On a Tuesday. Pray for someone who has not yet come to repentance: name them, and ask God to use today’s patience for them. And look back over your own life: list the years before you believed, or the seasons when you wandered, and see how long the Lord waited for you. That memory will make you patient with others.

For worship. He is not slow. He is patient. For centuries he has held back the day, not because he is weak or forgetful, but because he is long of temper and rich in mercy, and because there are still sheep of his to be brought home. He waited for the thief on the cross and for the persecutor on the Damascus road, and he waited for us. The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love. Every morning the world wakes and judgement has not fallen, the sun rises on a day of grace, given by a Saviour who will not lose one of those the Father gave him.

verseByVerse.quote: But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.

But the day of the Lord will come like a thief. “Day of the Lord” is the Old Testament term for God’s great day of judgement and salvation (Joel 2:31; Amos 5:18–20; Zephaniah 1:14–18), now identified with Christ’s return. “Like a thief”: suddenly, unexpectedly, without warning. The image is the Lord’s own (Matthew 24:43), and Paul and John use it too (1 Thessalonians 5:2; Revelation 16:15). What it conveys is not stealth for its own sake but unpredictability: the one thing about a burglary that you cannot prepare for is the timing. Not secretly, but unexpectedly. This thief does not come quietly; the next clause says the heavens will roar. And it answers the scoffers’ question exactly. They asked where the promise was; Peter says the promise includes the fact that you will not see it coming. Delay does not mean it will not come.

And then the heavens will pass away with a roar. “Pass away” (pareleusontai) is go by, disappear, the word Jesus used: heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away (Matthew 24:35). “With a roar” (rhoizēdon) is onomatopoeic: a rushing noise, a whizzing sound like an arrow in flight, the whirring of wings, the crackle of a great fire. Dramatic, sudden, audible. Peter’s universe does not end quietly.

And the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved. “Heavenly bodies” (stoicheia, elements) means either the basic elements of the physical world, or the sun, moon and stars (Isaiah 34:4). “Burned up” (kausoumena) is burning with intense heat. “Dissolved” (lythēsetai) is loosed, broken apart, the word for untying something. Either way the dissolution of the present order is total.

And the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed. Then the last clause, and it is the most important in the verse. “Exposed” (heurethēsetai) is will be found, laid bare, discovered. It changes the picture from mere destruction to disclosure. The fire is not chiefly an incinerator but a searchlight. Everything done on this earth will be brought into the open before God’s judgement (1 Corinthians 3:13; Hebrews 4:13). Nothing will be hidden. And that is a far more searching thought than annihilation would be. A universe that simply burns cancels the record; a universe that is laid bare produces it. Peter’s point against men who were living as they pleased on the assumption that nothing was coming is not only that the world will end but that it will be examined.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ at the end of this verse. The oldest read will be found or exposed (heurethēsetai); later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read will be burned up (katakaēsetai); some read will not be found. The more difficult reading, will be found, is most likely original, meaning laid bare before God’s judgement.

Where Christians differ: is the day of the Lord a single event? Dispensationalists often separate a secret rapture of the church from a later visible return, and place a thousand-year earthly kingdom between Christ’s return and the final judgement and new creation. Other premillennial Christians, who reject a secret rapture, still see a sequence: Christ’s return, a thousand-year reign, then the final judgement and new creation. Verdict: Peter places Christ’s coming, the day of the Lord, the judgement of the ungodly, and the dissolution of the present heavens and earth together in one great event, followed by the new heavens and new earth (vv. 7, 10, 12–13). This fits the amillennial understanding: one visible return of Christ, at which the dead are raised, all are judged, and creation is renewed. There is no secret rapture and no intervening earthly millennium.

If he comes like a thief, does that not mean a secret coming? No. The thief image describes the timing, not the manner. The same Lord who said he would come like a thief said that his coming would be like lightning flashing from east to west (Matthew 24:27), and that every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7). Here in Peter, the thief’s arrival is accompanied by the roar of the heavens. It will be sudden for everyone and secret to no one. That is why believers need not fear being left behind in a silent disappearance; we are called instead to be ready at any hour for a return that will fill the sky.

Will the earth then be annihilated, or renewed? Some Christians hold that the old creation will be destroyed and replaced, pointing to pass away and dissolved. But Peter compares it to the flood, which cleansed the world rather than abolishing it (v. 6), and says the earth will be exposed, laid bare to judgement. Paul says creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption (Romans 8:21). The more likely reading is that the present creation will be purged by fire and renewed, not abolished.

What it does not mean. It does not necessarily mean the universe will be annihilated and a new one created from nothing. Scripture speaks of the renewal of creation (Romans 8:19–21; Matthew 19:28; Acts 3:21). The fire purifies and transforms, like a refining fire, removing all that is sinful and corrupt.

Should I try to work out when it will happen? No. Jesus said that no one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36), and that it is not for us to know the times or seasons the Father has fixed (Acts 1:7). Every attempt to set dates has failed and brought the faith into ridicule. The signs Jesus gave (wars, false teachers, persecution, the gospel to the nations) mark the whole age, so that every generation should be ready. The right response to a thief who comes at an unknown hour is not to calculate the hour but to keep the house ready at all hours.

In a sentence. But the day of the Lord will come like a thief. The heavens will disappear with a roar; the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and everything done in it will be laid bare.

On a Tuesday. If Christ came today, what would be exposed in your life? Live in readiness, as one who will give account. Think of one thing you would hurry to hide if you knew he was coming tonight. Deal with it today: confess it, put it right, or remove it. Then you will be able to say, with an easier heart, come, Lord Jesus.

For worship. The heavens that declare the glory of God will roar at his coming, and the stars that have kept their courses since the beginning will be loosed by the hand that set them. Nothing will be hidden from him, and nothing that is his will be lost. For his people, the searchlight holds no terror, because everything it would find against them has already been found on Christ, and burned up in the fire of the cross. The day of the Lord is coming. It will be his day, the day the King comes into his own, and the earth that was laid bare will be made new.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — New Heavens, and the Last Command
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Since the present world will be dissolved and everything exposed before God, Peter asks what kind of people believers should be, and answers: holy and devoted to God, as they wait for the day of God and even hasten it. On that day the heavens will be set ablaze and dissolved, but believers look forward, as God promised, to new heavens and a new earth where righteousness is at home. So while they wait they should make every effort to be found by him at peace, spotless and blameless, and regard the Lord’s patience as an opportunity for salvation, as Paul also wrote with the wisdom God gave him, though some of his letters contain things hard to understand that unstable and untaught people twist, as they twist the rest of Scripture, to their own ruin. Forewarned, they must guard against being carried off by the error of the lawless, and instead grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be glory now and for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Answer to Error Is Growth

Since everything will be laid bare, live in holiness and godliness while waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells. The last command is to grow in the grace and knowledge of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter called Paul a beloved brother and counted his letters among the Scriptures.

Now: A growing believer is far harder to uproot than one who is merely on guard.

verseByVerse.quote: Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn! But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn! But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.

Since all these things are thus to be dissolved. “Dissolved” (lyomenōn) is a present participle: being loosed, as good as dissolving already. The present world is temporary. Everything you can see has a date stamped on it that you cannot read.

What sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness. Peter draws the practical conclusion, and it is worth noticing what he does not draw. Not speculation, not date-setting, not withdrawal. The question is about character. “What sort” (potapous) is what kind, how excellent. “Holiness” (hagiais anastrophais) is holy ways of life, and it is plural: in every area. “Godliness” (eusebeiais) is plural too: acts of godliness. Holy behaviours, godlinesses, which suggests the concrete and repeated rather than a general disposition. It is worked out in particular acts. Eschatology is not for speculation but for transformation. Belief in Christ’s return shapes holy living (1 John 3:2–3). If the house is to be pulled down, you do not spend your life polishing its brass; you invest in what will last.

Waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God. “Waiting for” (prosdokōntas) is expecting, looking for eagerly, as a family watches the road for a returning son. “Hastening” (speudontas) is startling. It can mean to be eager for, but its ordinary sense is to hurry, to speed something up. And Peter has just said the delay is God’s patience, waiting for people to reach repentance. Believers can, in some sense, hasten the day: by holy living, by prayer (your kingdom come, Matthew 6:10), and by evangelism, which brings in the elect whose conversion the Lord awaits (v. 9; Matthew 24:14). God has ordained the means as well as the end. That is a dignity given to ordinary Christian obedience which should stop anyone reading it casually.

Because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn! The description is repeated, and it is bleak, until verse 13 turns it round. “Melt” (tēketai), as in Isaiah 34:4 in the Greek, and Micah 1:4, where the mountains melt under the LORD like wax before the fire.

But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth. There is the point of the whole passage. “According to his promise” (kata to epangelma autou): Isaiah 65:17; 66:22. The scoffers asked, where is the promise? Peter answers: here it is. “New” (kainous) is new in quality, renewed, fresh: not merely a new universe in time, but a transformed one in kind (Revelation 21:1–5; Romans 8:19–21). The fire is not the end of the story, and it is not the destruction of the material world as such. What follows is a new earth: physical, real, and renewed, exactly as Isaiah promised, with resurrected people in resurrected bodies living in a world set free.

In which righteousness dwells. “Dwells” (katoikei) is settles down, makes its permanent home. In the present world, righteousness is a stranger, a visitor who is often turned away at the door; in the new creation, it will be at home. No more sin, injustice, evil or death (Revelation 21:4, 27). And that single clause is the answer to everything chapter 2 described. Peter has spent a chapter on men who exploited the church and seemed to get away with it. The world that is coming is one where righteousness is not visiting but resident, at home, which is the force of the verb. And righteousness at home means the Righteous One at home among his people: behold, the dwelling place of God is with man (Revelation 21:3).

What will the new heavens and new earth actually be like? Scripture gives us glimpses rather than a map, but the glimpses are glorious. It will be a real, physical world, this creation renewed, as our risen bodies will be these bodies glorified (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). God will dwell with his people; there will be no more tears, death, mourning or pain (Revelation 21:3–4). There will be work without frustration, worship without weariness, fellowship without sin, and the glory of the nations brought in (Revelation 21:24–26). Above all, we will see his face (Revelation 22:4). Whatever is good in this world will be there, freed from the curse, and Christ will be its light.

If this world will be dissolved, does it matter what I do with it now? Yes, very much. The new creation is this creation renewed, not discarded, so faithful work done in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). Caring for creation, doing justice, raising children, making things well, healing the sick: all of it honours the God who will renew the earth. What will not survive is sin, and whatever was done for self rather than for God (1 Corinthians 3:12–15). So hold this world loosely and serve it diligently: loosely, because it is passing; diligently, because it is his.

What it does not mean. Hastening does not mean we control God’s timetable or can force his hand. It means God uses his people’s prayers, holiness and witness in bringing about his purposes. Nor does a new creation mean the present world is worthless; it will be renewed, not discarded.

In a sentence. Since everything will be destroyed in this way, what kind of people ought you to be? You ought to live holy and godly lives as you look forward to the day of God and speed its coming. That day will bring about the destruction of the heavens by fire, and the elements will melt in the heat. But in keeping with his promise we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness is at home.

On a Tuesday. Pray your kingdom come today, and mean it. Then ask the question Peter asks: what sort of person ought I to be? Pick one concrete act of holiness and one act of godliness for today: an apology, an honest word, a generous gift, an hour of prayer, a conversation about Christ with someone who does not know him. Each one is a brick in a house that will not burn.

For worship. The fire is not the end. Beyond the roar and the melting is the promise: new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home, and where the Lord who was a stranger in his own world, who had nowhere to lay his head, will dwell with his people for ever. He makes all things new. He will wipe away every tear with his own hand. The creation that groaned will sing, the nations will walk in his light, and his servants will see his face. Everything Isaiah longed for, everything the martyrs died hoping for, he has promised, and he does not lie.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace. And count the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him, as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace. And count the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him, as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures.

Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these. “Waiting” (prosdokōntes), as in verse 12. Everything Peter now asks flows from that expectation. People who expect a wedding prepare for it.

Be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace. “Be diligent” (spoudasate) is make every effort, as in 1:5, 10: the letter’s word for earnest, grace-driven effort. “Found” (heurethēnai) picks up the word from verse 10, where the earth and its works are laid bare. The same verb, and the connection is deliberate: everything will be found out, so be diligent about what is found in you. When everything is exposed, be found in a good condition. “Without spot” (aspiloi) and “blemish” (amōmētoi) is another deliberate reversal: like Christ, the spotless Lamb (1 Peter 1:19), and the opposite of the false teachers, who are blots and blemishes at the church’s own feast (2:13). “At peace” (en eirēnē): at peace with God through Christ (Romans 5:1), and with one another.

How can I be found without spot or blemish when I still sin? In two ways. First, by standing in Christ: his spotless righteousness is counted as yours, and his blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). On that day you will be found in him, not having a righteousness of your own (Philippians 3:9). Second, by growing in holiness now, which is the fruit and evidence of being in him. Peter calls for diligence, not perfection. Keep short accounts with God, confess sin promptly, make peace with those you have wronged, and pursue holiness from a heart at rest in Christ’s finished work. He will present you blameless (Jude 24).

And count the patience of our Lord as salvation. Verse 9 restated as a command. “Count” (hēgeisthe) is regard, consider, reckon. The scoffers count it slowness (v. 9); believers count it salvation: every day of delay is a day of grace for more people to repent. The delay is not to be endured but reckoned, actively counted as mercy. It is the accounting verb, and Peter asks them to enter the interval on the right side of the ledger.

Just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him. “Beloved brother”: Peter’s warmth here is worth pausing on. These two men had a serious public disagreement at Antioch, where Paul opposed him to his face and later wrote it down for every church to read (Galatians 2:11–14). Peter calls him beloved brother and commends his wisdom. There is no trace of the quarrel. That is what grace does to an old wound. “Wisdom given him”: inspired wisdom, from God. Paul also taught about God’s patience leading to repentance (Romans 2:4; 9:22) and Christ’s return.

As he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. “All his letters”: Peter knew a collection of Paul’s letters, already circulating among the churches.

There are some things in them that are hard to understand. “Hard to understand” (dysnoēta) is difficult to grasp. A refreshingly honest admission from an apostle about another apostle, and a small comfort to anyone who has struggled through Romans. Some of Paul’s teaching, perhaps on grace, freedom, election, or the last things, requires careful thought.

Which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction. “Ignorant” (amatheis) is untaught, unlearned. “Unstable” (astēriktoi) is not established, as in 2:14. “Twist” (streblousin) is wrench, distort, torture as on a rack: making a text say what it never meant by force. The false teachers twisted Paul’s teaching on grace into a licence for immorality (Romans 3:8; 6:1). “To their own destruction”: misusing Scripture leads to ruin. Notice that difficulty is not the cause of the twisting: the ignorant and unstable are, and they do it to the plain parts too.

As they do the other Scriptures. “Other Scriptures” (tas loipas graphas). Peter already counts Paul’s letters among the Scriptures, alongside the Old Testament, while Paul was very likely still alive or only lately martyred. A remarkable early testimony to the recognition of the New Testament as inspired Scripture, within the apostolic generation itself. That is the New Testament recognising itself.

How can I avoid twisting Scripture? Read whole passages, not isolated verses, and ask what the author meant to his first readers before asking what it means for you. Let clear passages interpret harder ones. Read with the church: good preaching, sound commentaries, and the confessions of faith keep you from private eccentricities. Be especially careful when an interpretation happens to excuse what you already wanted to do; that was exactly the false teachers’ method. And come to the Bible humbly, ready to be corrected by it rather than to use it.

What it does not mean. Hard to understand does not mean Scripture is unclear in its main message, or that ordinary believers cannot read it. The gospel is clear (Psalm 19:7). It means some passages require careful, humble study, and that we must not twist them to suit ourselves.

In a sentence. So then, dear friends, since you are looking forward to this, make every effort to be found spotless, blameless and at peace with him. Bear in mind that our Lord’s patience means salvation, just as our dear brother Paul also wrote to you with the wisdom God gave him. He writes the same way in all his letters, speaking in them of these matters. His letters contain some things that are hard to understand, which ignorant and unstable people distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction.

On a Tuesday. When you read a hard passage of Scripture, study it humbly, in context, with good help. Never twist it to say what you want. And consider whether there is someone with whom you are not at peace, perhaps a fellow believer who once rebuked you publicly, as Paul did Peter. Follow Peter’s example: speak of them warmly, and seek peace.

For worship. The Lord’s patience is salvation. It saved the apostle who denied him, and the apostle who persecuted him, and it made the two of them beloved brothers who wrote, by the wisdom God gave them, the Scriptures we still read. It has saved us. And the same Lord who will lay the earth bare will find his people clothed in his own spotless righteousness, without spot or blemish, at peace. He was the Lamb without blemish, offered for blemished sinners, so that on the day everything is found out, we may be found in him.

verseByVerse.commentary:
You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, take care that you are not carried away with the error of lawless people and lose your own stability. But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.

You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand. “Knowing beforehand” (proginōskontes) is being forewarned. The whole letter’s purpose in a phrase. Peter has not written to inform them about the future but to prepare them, and forewarning is itself the protection. Forewarned is forearmed.

Take care that you are not carried away with the error of lawless people. “Take care” (phylassesthe) is guard yourselves, be on guard: a sentry’s word. “Carried away” (synapachthentes) is led away together with, swept along with, as a crowd sweeps along a man who did not intend to go. It is the word Paul used of Barnabas being carried away by Peter’s hypocrisy at Antioch (Galatians 2:13). Peter knew from his own failure how easily a good man is swept along, and how easily he can sweep others. “Error” (planē) is wandering, deception. “Lawless” (athesmōn) is unprincipled, the word used of the men of Sodom (2:7).

And lose your own stability. “Lose” (ekpesēte) is fall from. “Stability” (stērigmos) is firmness, steadfastness, from the same root as established (1:12) and unstable (v. 16; 2:14). A word has run through the letter: the unstable souls the false teachers baited (2:14), and the unstable who twist the Scriptures (3:16). Peter’s fear is that the steady will be pulled into that instability. And it is the word Jesus gave him: when you have turned again, strengthen (stērison) your brothers (Luke 22:32). His last sentence is still obeying that command.

But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Then the last command, and after two chapters of warning it is not what one expects. “Grow” (auxanete) is present tense: keep growing. The best defence against error is not merely avoiding it but growing in truth. Peter does not end by telling them to watch the heretics more closely; he tells them to get on with maturing. A tree that is growing is far harder to uproot than one being braced. And both nouns matter. “Grace”: God’s unmerited favour, experienced more and more deeply, because a man who forgets he was cleansed stops growing (1:9). “Knowledge”: personal knowledge of Christ (1:2–3, 8), the letter’s key word, reclaimed one last time from the men who were peddling a counterfeit. The answer to false knowledge is not less knowledge but the real thing, and it is knowledge of a person. The letter ends where it began (1:2).

How do I actually grow in grace? Grace is not a substance you collect but the favour of God in Christ, known more deeply. You grow in it by using the means God has given: his word read, heard and preached; prayer; the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of the church; and obedience, which opens the heart to know him more (John 14:21). You also grow through suffering and repentance, as each fresh sight of your need shows you more of his kindness. Growth is slow and often unseen, like a tree. Do not measure it day by day. Keep near the sources, and over years it will show.

What it does not mean. Lose your stability does not mean true believers can finally fall away. Peter has said they will never fall if they grow (1:10). The warning is one of God’s means to keep them standing.

To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen. “To him”: Jesus Christ. A doxology addressed to Christ, offering him the glory due to God alone, who says, my glory I give to no other (Isaiah 42:8). It is itself a statement about who he is, and a final testimony to his deity; the letter began by calling him our God and Saviour (1:1), and it ends by giving him God’s glory. “Day of eternity” (hēmera aiōnos) occurs nowhere else: the eternal day that begins at his return and never ends. Peter, having written a chapter about the day of the Lord and the day of judgement, ends by naming a day that has no evening. These are the last recorded words of the man who denied his Lord in a courtyard, written by someone who knew his death was near. He signs off with glory to the One he had once said he did not know.

In a sentence. Therefore, dear friends, since you have been forewarned, be on your guard so that you may not be carried away by the error of the lawless and fall from your secure position. But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be glory both now and for ever! Amen.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself whether you are more focused on what you are against than on growing in Christ. Spend more time this week with Christ himself than with arguments about error: read a Gospel chapter each day, and end each reading by giving him glory in your own words. And ask God to make you, like Peter, someone who strengthens others rather than sweeps them along.

For worship. The last word of Peter is glory, and the glory is Christ’s. The fisherman who sank in the waves, who cursed and swore that he did not know him, who was found and forgiven on a beach at dawn, ends his life with his eyes on the same Lord, now known as God and Saviour, now given the glory that belongs to God alone. That is what grace does. It takes a man who denied Jesus and makes him a pillar, and sends him to his cross singing doxology. To our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ be the glory, now, in the long patience of this age, and on the day of eternity that will never end. Amen.

3.theology:
Uniformitarianism and the Word of God: Peter's refutation of the scoffers in vv. 5–7 is a model of theological apologetics. The uniformitarians claim that the world operates by consistent natural processes. Peter grants the observation and then shows that the historical record — the record the uniformitarians themselves appeal to — contains two catastrophic interruptions of the very uniformity they invoke: creation and the flood. Both were brought about by the word of God. The same word that did those things has spoken again, and the third act — the fire — is as certain as the first two. The apologist who begins with Scripture's own historical witness is standing on solid ground.

Divine patience and the will of God in salvation: Verse 9 is one of the great texts on the scope of God's salvific will: 'not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.' Reformed theology reads this in its literary context: 'toward you' — the elect community. The 'all' is the full complement of those for whom God's patience is being exercised — all who will come to repentance within the span of his patience. This is not universalism (the Day will still come and shut the door), and it is not a contradiction of election (God's patience is itself the means by which the elect are gathered). It is the breathtaking truth that the apparent delay of the parousia is not divine procrastination — it is divine love, actively gathering those who are his.

New creation as promise: The new heavens and new earth of verse 13 is the eschatological horizon of the entire epistle — and of the entire New Testament. Herman Bavinck's axiom — grace restores nature — finds its ultimate expression here: the fire does not destroy the creation but purifies it; the new creation is this creation glorified, the world God made very good and will make even better. Anthony Hoekema's The Bible and the Future demonstrates that the new earth is not a replacement but a renewal — which is why Christian hope is not escapism but engagement: the world we tend and serve and love matters eternally, because it is the world God intends to redeem.
3.examples:
Then: The scoffers' question — 'Where is the promise of his coming?' — has been asked in every generation. The first generation of believers died; the second, the third, the hundredth. Each generation has faced the apparent delay, and the temptation to conclude that the promise was empty. Peter's answer remains the same across every generation: God is not slow. He is patient. His patience is not weakness — it is mercy in motion, gathering those who are still to be gathered before the door closes. Every generation of Christians lives in the overlap of promise and fulfilment, patience and urgency.

Now: 'What sort of people ought you to be?' (v. 11) is the most searching pastoral question the letter asks, and it lands as heavily today as it did in the first century. The return of Christ has not yet come — but it is coming, and it is certain. The question is not about calculation but about formation. The person who genuinely believes the Day is coming will live differently: with moral seriousness, with urgency about the gospel, with detachment from the world's false securities, with eager longing for righteousness. The Christian who has domesticated eschatology into a theological opinion without ethical bite has not yet let 2 Peter 3 do its work. Let it. Grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. That is the whole assignment — and it will last exactly until the Day of eternity.
